questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the dimensional formula of $\varepsilon_0$.
questions.solution:
Using Coulomb's law:

$F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$

Rearranging for $\varepsilon_0$:

$\varepsilon_0 = \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{4\pi F r^2}$

Substituting the dimensional formulas for charge $[q] = I T$, force $[F] = M L T^{-2}$, and distance $[r] = L$:

$[\varepsilon_0] = \dfrac{[I T] [I T]}{[M L T^{-2}] [L^2]}$

$[\varepsilon_0] = \dfrac{I^2 T^2}{M L^3 T^{-2}}$

$[\varepsilon_0] = M^{-1} L^{-3} T^4 I^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two equal charges are situated at a separation of $1.0 \text{ m}$. What must be the magnitude of the charges so that the force between them is equivalent to the weight of a $50 \text{ kg}$ person?
questions.solution:
Weight of the person, $W = mg = 50 \times 9.8 = 490 \text{ N}$

Electrostatic force between the charges, $F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q^2}{r^2}$

Substituting the given values:

$F = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times q^2}{1^2} = 9 \times 10^9 q^2$

Equating the electrostatic force to the weight:

$9 \times 10^9 q^2 = 490$

$q^2 = \dfrac{490}{9 \times 10^9} = 5.44 \times 10^{-8}$

$q = \sqrt{5.44 \times 10^{-8}} \approx 2.33 \times 10^{-4} \text{ C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the electric force between two protons separated by a distance of $1$ fermi ($1$ fermi $= 10^{-15} \text{ m}$). Protons within a nucleus remain at a separation of this order.
questions.solution:
Using Coulomb's law, the electric force between two protons is:

$F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$

Given $q_1 = q_2 = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ and $r = 10^{-15} \text{ m}$:

$F = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{(10^{-15})^2}$

$F = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 2.56 \times 10^{-38}}{10^{-30}}$

$F = 23.04 \times 10^1$

$F = 230.4 \text{ N}$

The force is approximately $230 \text{ N}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two charges of $2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ and $1.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ are located at a separation of $10 \text{ cm}$. Determine where a third charge must be placed so that it experiences zero net force from these two charges.
options: $3.3 \text{ cm}$ from the smaller charge, between the two charges
$5.9 \text{ cm}$ from the larger charge, between the two charges
$5.9 \text{ cm}$ from the smaller charge, between the two charges
$3.3 \text{ cm}$ from the larger charge, between the two charges
questions.solution:
Let the third charge $q$ be placed at a distance $x$ from the larger charge $q_1 = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$.

The distance from the smaller charge $q_2 = 1.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ will be $(10 - x) \text{ cm}$.

For the net force on $q$ to be zero, the electrostatic forces due to $q_1$ and $q_2$ must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction:

$\dfrac{k q_1 q}{x^2} = \dfrac{k q_2 q}{(10 - x)^2}$

Substituting the given values:

$\dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-6}}{x^2} = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-6}}{(10 - x)^2}$

$\dfrac{2}{x^2} = \dfrac{1}{(10 - x)^2}$

Taking the square root of both sides:

$\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{x} = \dfrac{1}{10 - x}$

$10\sqrt{2} - \sqrt{2}x = x$

$x(\sqrt{2} + 1) = 10\sqrt{2}$

$x = \dfrac{10\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2} + 1}$

Rationalizing the denominator:

$x = 10\sqrt{2}(\sqrt{2} - 1) = 20 - 10\sqrt{2}$

Using $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$:

$x = 20 - 14.14 = 5.86 \text{ cm}$

Rounding to one decimal place, we get $x \approx 5.9 \text{ cm}$ from the larger charge.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A $1.0 \text{ C}$ charge is positioned at the top of a college building, while another equal charge is located at the top of a house. Assuming the separation between the two charges to be $2.0 \text{ km}$, determine the force they exert on each other.
questions.solution:
According to Coulomb's law, the electrostatic force between two point charges is given by

$F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$

Given:
$q_1 = 1.0 \text{ C}$
$q_2 = 1.0 \text{ C}$
$r = 2.0 \text{ km} = 2.0 \times 10^3 \text{ m}$
$\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \text{ N m}^2/\text{C}^2$

Substituting the values into the formula:

$F = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 1.0 \times 1.0}{(2.0 \times 10^3)^2}$

$F = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9}{4.0 \times 10^6}$

$F = 2.25 \times 10^3 \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the separation at which two equal charges of $1.0 \text{ C}$ each must be placed so that the force between them is equal to the weight of a $50 \text{ kg}$ person.
questions.solution:
The electrostatic force between two charges is given by Coulomb's law:

$F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$

The weight of the person is given by:

$W = mg$

Equating the electrostatic force to the weight of the person:

$\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2} = mg$

Substituting the given values ($q_1 = q_2 = 1.0 \text{ C}$, $m = 50 \text{ kg}$, $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$, $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \text{ N m}^2/\text{C}^2$):

$\dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 1.0 \times 1.0}{r^2} = 50 \times 9.8$

$\dfrac{9 \times 10^9}{r^2} = 490$

$r^2 = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9}{490} = \dfrac{900}{49} \times 10^6$

$r = \dfrac{30}{7} \times 10^3 \approx 4.28 \times 10^3 \text{ m}$

Rounding to two significant figures, we get $4.3 \times 10^3 \text{ m}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two charges of $2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ and $-1.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ are placed at a separation of $10 \text{ cm}$. Determine the position where a third charge will experience zero net force.
options: $34.1 \text{ cm}$ from the larger magnitude charge on the side of the smaller magnitude charge
$14.1 \text{ cm}$ from the larger magnitude charge on the side of the smaller magnitude charge
$5.9 \text{ cm}$ from the larger magnitude charge between the two charges
$24.1 \text{ cm}$ from the larger magnitude charge on the side of the smaller magnitude charge
questions.solution:
Let $q_1 = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ and $q_2 = -1.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$.

The distance between the charges is $d = 10 \text{ cm}$.

For the net force on a third charge to be zero, the net electric field at that point must be zero. Since the charges have opposite signs, the neutral point lies on the line joining the charges, outside the region between them, and closer to the charge with the smaller magnitude ($q_2$).

Let the neutral point be at a distance $x$ from $q_1$ on the side of $q_2$. The distance of this point from $q_2$ is $x - 10$.

Equating the magnitudes of the electric fields produced by $q_1$ and $q_2$ at this point:

$\dfrac{k |q_1|}{x^2} = \dfrac{k |q_2|}{(x - 10)^2}$

$\dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-6}}{x^2} = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-6}}{(x - 10)^2}$

$\dfrac{2}{x^2} = \dfrac{1}{(x - 10)^2}$

Taking the square root of both sides:

$\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{x} = \dfrac{1}{x - 10}$

$\sqrt{2} (x - 10) = x$

$x (\sqrt{2} - 1) = 10 \sqrt{2}$

$x = \dfrac{10 \sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2} - 1}$

Rationalizing the denominator:

$x = 10 \sqrt{2} (\sqrt{2} + 1) = 10 (2 + \sqrt{2})$

Using $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$:

$x = 10 (2 + 1.414) = 34.14 \text{ cm}$

The position is $34.1 \text{ cm}$ from the larger magnitude charge on the side of the smaller magnitude charge.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two charged particles are separated by a distance of $1.0 \text{ cm}$. Determine the minimum possible magnitude of the electric force acting on each charge.
questions.solution:
The electric force between two charges $q_1$ and $q_2$ separated by a distance $r$ is given by Coulomb's law:

$F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$

For the force to be minimum, the charges must have the minimum possible magnitude. The minimum possible charge on a particle is the elementary charge $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.

Given the separation distance $r = 1.0 \text{ cm} = 10^{-2} \text{ m}$, substituting the values into the formula:

$F = \dfrac{(9 \times 10^9) \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{(10^{-2})^2}$

$F = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 2.56 \times 10^{-38}}{10^{-4}}$

$F = 23.04 \times 10^{-25} \text{ N}$

$F \approx 2.3 \times 10^{-24} \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Estimate the number of electrons contained in $100 \text{ g}$ of water. What is the total negative charge of these electrons?
questions.solution:
Molecular mass of water ($H_2O$) is $18 \text{ g/mol}$.

Number of moles in $100 \text{ g}$ of water is $\dfrac{100}{18} \text{ mol}$.

Number of molecules in $100 \text{ g}$ of water is $\dfrac{100}{18} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} \approx 3.345 \times 10^{24}$.

Each molecule of water ($H_2O$) contains $2 + 8 = 10$ electrons.

Total number of electrons is $10 \times 3.345 \times 10^{24} = 3.345 \times 10^{25} \approx 3.35 \times 10^{25}$.

The magnitude of charge on one electron is $1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.

Total negative charge is $3.345 \times 10^{25} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \approx 5.35 \times 10^6 \text{ C}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Assume a gold nucleus is a sphere of radius $6.9$ fermi in which protons and neutrons are distributed. Determine the repulsive force between two protons located at the maximum possible separation. Why do the protons not fly apart under such repulsion?
options: $1.2 \text{ N}$, due to the weak nuclear force
$4.8 \text{ N}$, due to the gravitational force
$1.2 \text{ N}$, due to the strong nuclear force
$4.8 \text{ N}$, due to the strong nuclear force
questions.solution:
The maximum possible separation between two protons in the nucleus is its diameter.

$r = 2R = 2 \times 6.9 \text{ fm} = 13.8 \times 10^{-15} \text{ m}$

The electrostatic repulsive force between the protons is given by Coulomb's law:

$F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q^2}{r^2}$

Substituting the values:

$F = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{(13.8 \times 10^{-15})^2}$

$F = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 2.56 \times 10^{-38}}{190.44 \times 10^{-30}}$

$F \approx 1.2 \text{ N}$

The protons do not fly apart because the attractive strong nuclear force between nucleons is much stronger than the electrostatic repulsion at these distances.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two insulating small spheres are rubbed together and then positioned $1 \text{ cm}$ apart. If they attract one another with a force of $0.1 \text{ N}$, determine the approximate number of electrons transferred from one sphere to the other during the rubbing process.
questions.solution:
When two spheres are rubbed together, they acquire equal and opposite charges. Let the number of electrons transferred be $n$.

The magnitude of charge on each sphere is $q = ne$.

Using Coulomb's law, the force of attraction is given by:

$F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q^2}{r^2}$

Substituting the given values $F = 0.1 \text{ N}$ and $r = 1 \text{ cm} = 10^{-2} \text{ m}$:

$0.1 = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times q^2}{(10^{-2})^2}$

$0.1 = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times q^2}{10^{-4}}$

$q^2 = \dfrac{0.1 \times 10^{-4}}{9 \times 10^9} = \dfrac{10^{-5}}{9 \times 10^9} = \dfrac{1}{9} \times 10^{-14}$

$q = \dfrac{1}{3} \times 10^{-7} \text{ C}$

Since $q = ne$, the number of electrons transferred is:

$n = \dfrac{q}{e} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{3} \times 10^{-7}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}}$

$n = \dfrac{10^{-7}}{4.8 \times 10^{-19}} = \dfrac{10^{12}}{4.8} \approx 2.08 \times 10^{11}$

The approximate number of electrons transferred is $2 \times 10^{11}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Assume all the electrons in $100 \text{ g}$ of water are lumped together to form a negatively charged particle, while all the nuclei are lumped together to form a positively charged particle. If these two particles are situated $10.0 \text{ cm}$ apart, determine the force of attraction between them. (Consider how this compares with your own weight).
questions.solution:
Molar mass of water ($H_2O$) is $18 \text{ g/mol}$.

Number of moles in $100 \text{ g}$ of water = $\dfrac{100}{18}$.

Taking Avogadro's number $N_A = 6 \times 10^{23} \text{ mol}^{-1}$, the number of water molecules is:

$N = \dfrac{100}{18} \times 6 \times 10^{23} = \dfrac{10^{25}}{3}$

Each water molecule contains $10$ electrons and $10$ protons.

Total number of electrons = $10 \times \dfrac{10^{25}}{3} = \dfrac{10^{26}}{3}$.

Total negative charge $q_1 = -\dfrac{10^{26}}{3} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = -\dfrac{1.6 \times 10^7}{3} \text{ C}$.

Total positive charge $q_2 = +\dfrac{1.6 \times 10^7}{3} \text{ C}$.

Distance between the charges $r = 10.0 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$.

Force of attraction $F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2}$.

$F = 9 \times 10^9 \times \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{1.6 \times 10^7}{3}\right)^2}{(0.1)^2}$

$F = 9 \times 10^9 \times \dfrac{2.56 \times 10^{14}}{9} \times 100$

$F = 2.56 \times 10^{25} \text{ N}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An NaCl molecule is bound by the electric force between the sodium and chlorine ions when one electron from sodium is transferred to chlorine. Assuming the ions act as point charges and taking the separation between them to be $2.75 \times 10^{-8} \text{ cm}$, determine the force of attraction between them.
questions.solution:
The charges on the sodium and chlorine ions are $+e$ and $-e$ respectively, where $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.

The separation between the ions is $r = 2.75 \times 10^{-8} \text{ cm} = 2.75 \times 10^{-10} \text{ m}$.

Using Coulomb's law, the force of attraction is given by:

$F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$

Substituting the values:

$F = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{(2.75 \times 10^{-10})^2}$

$F = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 2.56 \times 10^{-38}}{7.5625 \times 10^{-20}}$

$F = \dfrac{23.04 \times 10^{-29}}{7.5625 \times 10^{-20}}$

$F \approx 3.05 \times 10^{-9} \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the ratio of the electric and gravitational forces between two protons.
questions.solution:
The electric force between two protons separated by a distance $r$ is given by Coulomb's law:

$F_e = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{e^2}{r^2}$

The gravitational force between them is given by Newton's law of gravitation:

$F_g = G \dfrac{m_p^2}{r^2}$

The ratio of the two forces is:

$\dfrac{F_e}{F_g} = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 G m_p^2}$

Substituting the standard values:

$e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$

$\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \text{ N m}^2/\text{C}^2$

$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2/\text{kg}^2$

$m_p = 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$

$\dfrac{F_e}{F_g} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times (1.67 \times 10^{-27})^2}$

$\dfrac{F_e}{F_g} = \dfrac{9 \times 2.56 \times 10^{-29}}{6.67 \times 2.7889 \times 10^{-65}}$

$\dfrac{F_e}{F_g} = \dfrac{23.04}{18.60} \times 10^{36} \approx 1.23 \times 10^{36}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider an attractive nuclear force acting between two protons that can be expressed as $F = Ce^{-kr}/r^2$. Determine the dimensional formulae and appropriate SI units of $C$ and $k$.
questions.solution:
The given equation is $F = \dfrac{C e^{-kr}}{r^2}$.

Since the exponent of an exponential function must be dimensionless, the term $kr$ is dimensionless.

$[k][r] = [M^0 L^0 T^0]$

$[k] = \dfrac{1}{[r]} = [L^{-1}]$

The SI unit of $k$ is $\text{m}^{-1}$.

The exponential term $e^{-kr}$ is dimensionless, so the dimensions of $F$ and $\dfrac{C}{r^2}$ must be the same.

$[F] = \dfrac{[C]}{[r^2]}$

$[C] = [F][r^2] = [M L T^{-2}][L^2] = [M L^3 T^{-2}]$

The SI unit of $C$ is $\text{N m}^2$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider an attractive nuclear force acting between two protons that can be expressed as $F = Ce^{-kr}/r^2$. Assume that $k = 1 \text{ fermi}^{-1}$ and the repulsive electric force between the protons is exactly balanced by the attractive nuclear force at a separation of $5 \text{ fermi}$. Determine the value of $C$.
questions.solution:
The repulsive electric force between two protons is given by Coulomb's law:

$F_{e} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{e^2}{r^2}$

The attractive nuclear force is given by:

$F_{n} = C \dfrac{e^{-kr}}{r^2}$

At $r = 5 \text{ fermi}$, these forces balance each other, so $F_{e} = F_{n}$.

$\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{e^2}{r^2} = C \dfrac{e^{-kr}}{r^2}$

$C = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0} e^{kr}$

Given $k = 1 \text{ fermi}^{-1}$ and $r = 5 \text{ fermi}$, we have $kr = 5$.

Substituting the known values:

$\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \text{ N m}^2/\text{C}^2$

$e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$

$e^5 \approx 148.4$

$C = (9 \times 10^9) \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2 \times e^5$

$C = 9 \times 10^9 \times 2.56 \times 10^{-38} \times 148.4$

$C = 23.04 \times 10^{-29} \times 148.4$

$C \approx 3419 \times 10^{-29} \text{ N m}^2$

$C \approx 3.4 \times 10^{-26} \text{ N m}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three identical charges, each of $2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$, are held fixed at the three corners of an equilateral triangle of side $5 \text{ cm}$. Determine the magnitude of the Coulomb force experienced by one of the charges due to the other two.
questions.solution:
Let the charges be placed at the vertices of the equilateral triangle. The force exerted by one charge on another at a distance $a$ is given by Coulomb's law:

$F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q^2}{a^2}$

Substituting the given values $q = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ and $a = 5 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$:

$F = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times (2.0 \times 10^{-6})^2}{(5 \times 10^{-2})^2}$

$F = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-12}}{25 \times 10^{-4}} = \dfrac{36 \times 10^{-3}}{25 \times 10^{-4}} = 14.4 \text{ N}$

The charge at any vertex experiences two such forces from the other two charges. Since the triangle is equilateral, the angle between these two forces is $60^{\circ}$.

The magnitude of the resultant force is:

$F_{net} = \sqrt{F^2 + F^2 + 2F^2 \cos 60^{\circ}}$

$F_{net} = \sqrt{2F^2 + 2F^2 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)} = \sqrt{3F^2} = F\sqrt{3}$

$F_{net} = 14.4 \times \sqrt{3} \approx 14.4 \times 1.732 \approx 24.9 \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Four identical charges of $2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ each are secured at the four corners of a square with a side length of $5 \text{ cm}$. Determine the Coulomb force experienced by one of the charges due to the remaining three.
options: $14.4 \text{ N}$ directed at $45^\circ$ to the extended sides of the square
$27.5 \text{ N}$ directed at $45^\circ$ to the extended sides of the square
$20.4 \text{ N}$ directed at $45^\circ$ to the extended sides of the square
$36.0 \text{ N}$ directed at $45^\circ$ to the extended sides of the square
questions.solution:
Let the four charges $q = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ be placed at the corners A, B, C, and D of a square of side $a = 0.05 \text{ m}$.

We calculate the net force on the charge at corner D due to the charges at A, B, and C.

The force due to the charge at A is directed along AD:

$F_A = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q^2}{a^2} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times (2.0 \times 10^{-6})^2}{(0.05)^2} = 14.4 \text{ N}$

The force due to the charge at C is directed along CD:

$F_C = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q^2}{a^2} = 14.4 \text{ N}$

The force due to the charge at B is directed along the diagonal BD:

$F_B = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q^2}{(\sqrt{2}a)^2} = \dfrac{F_A}{2} = 7.2 \text{ N}$

The forces $F_A$ and $F_C$ are perpendicular to each other. Their resultant $F_{AC}$ is directed along the diagonal BD:

$F_{AC} = \sqrt{F_A^2 + F_C^2} = 14.4\sqrt{2} \approx 20.36 \text{ N}$

Since $F_{AC}$ and $F_B$ are in the same direction, the net force on the charge at D is:

$F_{net} = F_{AC} + F_B = 20.36 + 7.2 = 27.56 \text{ N} \approx 27.5 \text{ N}$

The resultant force is directed along the diagonal, which makes an angle of $45^\circ$ with the extended sides of the square.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A hydrogen atom consists of one proton and one electron. It may be assumed that the electron revolves in a circle of radius $0.53$ angstrom ($1$ angstrom $= 10^{-10} \text{ m}$ and is abbreviated as Å) with the proton positioned at the centre. The hydrogen atom is said to be in the ground state in this scenario. Determine the magnitude of the electric force between the proton and the electron of a hydrogen atom in its ground state.
questions.solution:
The magnitude of the electric force between the proton and the electron is given by Coulomb's law:

$F = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} \dfrac{e^2}{r^2}$

Substituting the values $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, $r = 0.53 \times 10^{-10} \text{ m}$, and $\dfrac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \text{ N m}^2 \text{ C}^{-2}$:

$F = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{(0.53 \times 10^{-10})^2}$

$F = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 2.56 \times 10^{-38}}{0.2809 \times 10^{-20}}$

$F = \dfrac{23.04 \times 10^{-29}}{0.2809 \times 10^{-20}}$

$F \approx 82.02 \times 10^{-9} \text{ N}$

$F \approx 8.2 \times 10^{-8} \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A hydrogen atom comprises one proton and one electron. We can assume that the electron revolves in a circle of radius $0.53$ angstrom ($1$ angstrom $= 10^{-10} \text{ m}$, abbreviated as Å) with the proton situated at the centre. Under these conditions, the hydrogen atom is considered to be in the ground state. Determine the speed of the electron in the ground state of a hydrogen atom.
questions.solution:
The centripetal force for the circular motion of the electron is provided by the electrostatic force of attraction between the proton and the electron.

$\dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{e^2}{r^2}$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 mr}}$

Substituting the standard values $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, $m = 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$, $r = 0.53 \times 10^{-10} \text{ m}$, and $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \text{ N m}^2/\text{C}^2$:

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 0.53 \times 10^{-10}}}$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{23.04 \times 10^{-29}}{4.823 \times 10^{-41}}}$

$v = \sqrt{4.77 \times 10^{12}}$

$v = 2.18 \times 10^6 \text{ m/s}$

Alternatively, using Bohr's quantization condition for the ground state ($n=1$):

$mvr = \dfrac{h}{2\pi}$

$v = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{2 \times 3.14 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 0.53 \times 10^{-10}} = 2.18 \times 10^6 \text{ m/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Ten positively charged particles are held fixed along the $x$-axis at positions $x = 10 \text{ cm}, 20 \text{ cm}, 30 \text{ cm}, \ldots, 100 \text{ cm}$. The first particle possesses a charge of $1.0 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C}$, the second $8 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C}$, the third $27 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C}$, and so forth, up to the tenth particle which has a charge of $1000 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C}$. Determine the magnitude of the electric force acting on a $1 \text{ C}$ charge located at the origin.
questions.solution:
The position of the $n^{\text{th}}$ particle is $x_n = n \times 10 \text{ cm} = n \times 0.1 \text{ m}$.

The charge of the $n^{\text{th}}$ particle follows the pattern $q_n = n^3 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C}$.

The electric force exerted by the $n^{\text{th}}$ particle on a $1 \text{ C}$ charge at the origin is given by Coulomb's law:

$F_n = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{Q q_n}{x_n^2}$

Substituting the given values:

$F_n = (9 \times 10^9) \dfrac{1 \times (n^3 \times 10^{-8})}{(n \times 0.1)^2}$

$F_n = (9 \times 10^9) \dfrac{n^3 \times 10^{-8}}{n^2 \times 10^{-2}}$

$F_n = 9 \times 10^9 \times n \times 10^{-6} = 9 \times 10^3 n \text{ N}$

The total electric force $F$ is the sum of the forces from all $10$ particles:

$F = \sum_{n=1}^{10} F_n = \sum_{n=1}^{10} 9 \times 10^3 n$

$F = 9 \times 10^3 \sum_{n=1}^{10} n$

Using the formula for the sum of the first $n$ natural numbers, $\sum_{n=1}^{10} n = \dfrac{10 \times 11}{2} = 55$:

$F = 9 \times 10^3 \times 55$

$F = 495 \times 10^3 \text{ N}$

$F = 4.95 \times 10^5 \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Placed on a smooth horizontal table, two charged particles, each with a charge of $2.0 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C}$, are connected by an insulating string of length $1 \text{ m}$. Determine the tension in the string.
questions.solution:
The tension in the string balances the electrostatic force of repulsion between the two charged particles.

Using Coulomb's law, the electrostatic force is given by:

$F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$

Substituting the given values $q_1 = q_2 = 2.0 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C}$ and $r = 1 \text{ m}$:

$F = 9 \times 10^9 \times \dfrac{(2.0 \times 10^{-8}) \times (2.0 \times 10^{-8})}{1^2}$

$F = 9 \times 10^9 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-16}$

$F = 36 \times 10^{-7} \text{ N}$

$F = 3.6 \times 10^{-6} \text{ N}$

Therefore, the tension in the string is $3.6 \times 10^{-6} \text{ N}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical balls, each possessing a charge of $2.00 \times 10^{-7} \text{ C}$ and a mass of $100 \text{ g}$, are suspended by two $50 \text{ cm}$ long insulating strings from a common point. The balls are initially held $5.0 \text{ cm}$ apart and subsequently released. Determine the electric force on one of the charged balls at the instant just after release.
questions.solution:
The electric force between two point charges is given by Coulomb's law:

$F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$

Given that the charges on the balls are $q_1 = q_2 = 2.00 \times 10^{-7} \text{ C}$ and the initial separation is $r = 5.0 \text{ cm} = 5.0 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$.

Substituting the given values into the formula:

$F = \dfrac{(9 \times 10^9) \times (2.00 \times 10^{-7})^2}{(5.0 \times 10^{-2})^2}$

$F = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 4.00 \times 10^{-14}}{25 \times 10^{-4}}$

$F = \dfrac{36 \times 10^{-5}}{25 \times 10^{-4}}$

$F = 1.44 \times 10^{-1} \text{ N} = 0.144 \text{ N}$

The mass of the balls and the length of the strings do not affect the magnitude of the electric force at the instant of release.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical balls, each possessing a charge of $2.00 \times 10^{-7} \text{ C}$ and a mass of $100 \text{ g}$, are suspended by two $50 \text{ cm}$ long insulating strings from a common point. The balls are initially held $5.0 \text{ cm}$ apart and subsequently released. Determine the components of the resultant force on one of the balls along and perpendicular to the string at the instant just after release.
options: $0.095 \text{ N}$ along the string, zero perpendicular to the string
$0.986 \text{ N}$ along the string, $0.095 \text{ N}$ perpendicular to the string towards the other charge
Zero along the string, $0.144 \text{ N}$ perpendicular to the string away from the other charge
Zero along the string, $0.095 \text{ N}$ perpendicular to the string away from the other charge
questions.solution:
The forces acting on each ball are the tension $T$ in the string, the gravitational force $mg$, and the electrostatic repulsion $F_e$.

Just after release, the velocity of the balls is zero, which means the centripetal acceleration is zero. Therefore, the net force along the string is zero.

The electrostatic force between the balls is:

$F_e = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q^2}{d^2} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times (2.00 \times 10^{-7})^2}{(0.05)^2} = 0.144 \text{ N}$

Let $\theta$ be the angle the string makes with the vertical. The distance from the vertical axis to each ball is $\dfrac{d}{2} = 2.5 \text{ cm}$.

$\sin\theta = \dfrac{2.5}{50} = 0.05$

For small angles, $\cos\theta \approx 1$.

The component of gravity perpendicular to the string (directed towards the other charge) is:

$mg \sin\theta = 0.1 \times 9.8 \times 0.05 = 0.049 \text{ N}$

The component of the electrostatic force perpendicular to the string (directed away from the other charge) is:

$F_e \cos\theta = 0.144 \times 1 = 0.144 \text{ N}$

The net force perpendicular to the string is:

$F_{\perp} = F_e \cos\theta - mg \sin\theta = 0.144 - 0.049 = 0.095 \text{ N}$

Since $F_e \cos\theta > mg \sin\theta$, the resultant force is directed away from the other charge.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical balls, each possessing a charge of $2.00 \times 10^{-7} \text{ C}$ and a mass of $100 \text{ g}$, are suspended by two $50 \text{ cm}$ long insulating strings from a common point. The balls are initially held $5.0 \text{ cm}$ apart and subsequently released. Determine the tension in the string at the instant just after release.
questions.solution:
Let $\theta$ be the angle made by the string with the vertical. The distance between the balls is $x = 5.0 \text{ cm} = 0.05 \text{ m}$, and the length of the string is $L = 50 \text{ cm} = 0.5 \text{ m}$.

From the geometry of the suspension:
$\sin\theta = \dfrac{x/2}{L} = \dfrac{0.025}{0.5} = 0.05$
$\cos\theta = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2\theta} = \sqrt{1 - (0.05)^2} = \sqrt{0.9975} \approx 0.99875$

The electrostatic force of repulsion between the balls is:
$F_e = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q^2}{x^2} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times (2.00 \times 10^{-7})^2}{(0.05)^2}$
$F_e = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 4 \times 10^{-14}}{0.0025} = 0.144 \text{ N}$

The weight of each ball is:
$mg = 0.1 \text{ kg} \times 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2 = 0.98 \text{ N}$

Just after release, the velocity of the balls is zero, which means the centripetal (radial) acceleration is zero. Therefore, the net force along the string must be zero.

Balancing the forces along the string:
$T - mg \cos\theta - F_e \sin\theta = 0$
$T = mg \cos\theta + F_e \sin\theta$

Substituting the values:
$T = (0.98 \times 0.99875) + (0.144 \times 0.05)$
$T = 0.978775 + 0.0072 = 0.985975 \text{ N}$

Rounding off to three significant figures, we get $T \approx 0.986 \text{ N}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical balls, each possessing a charge of $2.00 \times 10^{-7} \text{ C}$ and a mass of $100 \text{ g}$, are suspended by two $50 \text{ cm}$ long insulating strings from a common point. The balls are initially held $5.0 \text{ cm}$ apart and subsequently released. Determine the acceleration of one of the balls at the instant just after release.
options: $0.95 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ perpendicular to the string, away from the other charge
$1.44 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ horizontally, away from the other charge
$0.95 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ perpendicular to the string, towards the other charge
questions.solution:
The forces acting on each ball are the electrostatic force $F_e$, the gravitational force $mg$, and the tension $T$ in the string.

Since the balls are released from rest, the initial velocity is zero. Thus, the radial acceleration is zero, and the net acceleration is purely tangential (perpendicular to the string).

The electrostatic force between the balls is given by Coulomb's law:

$F_e = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q^2}{d^2}$

$F_e = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times (2.00 \times 10^{-7})^2}{(0.05)^2} = 0.144 \text{ N}$

The angle $\theta$ made by each string with the vertical is:

$\sin \theta = \dfrac{d/2}{L} = \dfrac{2.5 \text{ cm}}{50 \text{ cm}} = 0.05$

For this small angle, $\cos \theta \approx 1$.

The tangential component of the net force is:

$F_t = F_e \cos \theta - mg \sin \theta$

$F_t = 0.144 \times 1 - (0.1 \times 9.8 \times 0.05) = 0.144 - 0.049 = 0.095 \text{ N}$

The tangential acceleration of the ball is:

$a = \dfrac{F_t}{m} = \dfrac{0.095}{0.1} = 0.95 \text{ m s}^{-2}$

Since $F_e \cos \theta > mg \sin \theta$, the net force and acceleration are directed perpendicular to the string, away from the other charge.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical pith balls are charged by rubbing against one another. They are suspended from a horizontal rod using two strings of length $20 \text{ cm}$ each, with a separation of $5 \text{ cm}$ between the suspension points. In equilibrium, the separation between the balls is $3 \text{ cm}$. Determine the mass of each ball and the tension in the strings. The charge on each ball has a magnitude of $2.0 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C}$.
questions.solution:
When the two identical pith balls are rubbed against each other, they acquire equal and opposite charges, leading to an electrostatic force of attraction between them.

The electrostatic force of attraction is given by Coulomb's law:
$F_e = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q^2}{r^2}$

Substituting the given values:
$F_e = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times (2.0 \times 10^{-8})^2}{(0.03)^2} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-16}}{9 \times 10^{-4}} = 4.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ N}$

Let $\theta$ be the angle made by each string with the vertical. The suspension points are $5 \text{ cm}$ apart, and the balls are $3 \text{ cm}$ apart in equilibrium. By symmetry, the horizontal displacement of each ball from the vertical line passing through its suspension point is:
$x = \dfrac{5 \text{ cm} - 3 \text{ cm}}{2} = 1 \text{ cm}$

The length of each string is $L = 20 \text{ cm}$. Thus, we have:
$\sin\theta = \dfrac{x}{L} = \dfrac{1}{20} = 0.05$

The cosine of the angle is:
$\cos\theta = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2\theta} = \sqrt{1 - (0.05)^2} = \sqrt{0.9975} \approx 0.9987$

In equilibrium, the horizontal component of the tension balances the electrostatic force, and the vertical component balances the weight of the ball:
$T \sin\theta = F_e$
$T \cos\theta = mg$

From the first equilibrium condition, the tension $T$ in the string is:
$T = \dfrac{F_e}{\sin\theta} = \dfrac{4.0 \times 10^{-3}}{0.05} = 8.0 \times 10^{-2} \text{ N}$

From the second equilibrium condition, the mass $m$ of each ball is:
$m = \dfrac{T \cos\theta}{g}$

Taking $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$:
$m = \dfrac{8.0 \times 10^{-2} \times 0.9987}{9.8} \approx 8.15 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg} = 8.15 \text{ g}$

Rounding to two significant figures, the mass is approximately $8.2 \text{ g}$.

Answer: $8.2 \text{ g}$, $8.0 \times 10^{-2} \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two small spheres, each with a mass of $20 \text{ g}$, are hung from a common point by two insulating strings, each $40 \text{ cm}$ long. The spheres carry identical charges, and the equilibrium separation between the balls is observed to be $4 \text{ cm}$. Determine the charge on each sphere.
questions.solution:
Let the charge on each sphere be $q$.

The forces acting on each sphere in equilibrium are the tension $T$ in the string, the weight $mg$ acting downwards, and the electrostatic force of repulsion $F_e$ acting horizontally.

Resolving the tension into horizontal and vertical components:
$T \sin \theta = F_e$
$T \cos \theta = mg$

Dividing the two equations, we get:
$\tan \theta = \dfrac{F_e}{mg}$

From the geometry of the arrangement, the distance of each sphere from the vertical axis is $\dfrac{x}{2} = \dfrac{4 \text{ cm}}{2} = 2 \text{ cm} = 0.02 \text{ m}$.
Since the angle $\theta$ is very small, $\tan \theta \approx \sin \theta = \dfrac{0.02}{0.40} = 0.05$.

The electrostatic force is given by Coulomb's law:
$F_e = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q^2}{x^2} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times q^2}{(0.04)^2}$

Substituting the values into the equilibrium condition:
$\dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times q^2}{0.0016} = mg \tan \theta$

Using $m = 20 \text{ g} = 0.02 \text{ kg}$ and $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$:
$\dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times q^2}{0.0016} = 0.02 \times 9.8 \times 0.05$

$\dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times q^2}{0.0016} = 0.0098$

$q^2 = \dfrac{0.0098 \times 0.0016}{9 \times 10^9}$

$q^2 = \dfrac{15.68 \times 10^{-6}}{9 \times 10^9} = 1.742 \times 10^{-15} = 17.42 \times 10^{-16} \text{ C}^2$

$q = \sqrt{17.42 \times 10^{-16}} \approx 4.17 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical pith balls, each with a charge $q$, are suspended from a common point using two strings of equal length $l$. Determine the mass of each ball given that the angle between the strings is $2\theta$ in equilibrium.
questions.solution:
The angle made by each string with the vertical is $\theta$.

Distance between the two balls, $r = 2l \sin\theta$.

Electrostatic force of repulsion between the balls, $F_e = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{q^2}{r^2} = \dfrac{q^2}{16\pi\varepsilon_0 l^2 \sin^2\theta}$.

For the equilibrium of each ball, balancing the forces in the horizontal and vertical directions:

$T \sin\theta = F_e$

$T \cos\theta = mg$

Dividing the two equations:

$\tan\theta = \dfrac{F_e}{mg}$

$m = \dfrac{F_e}{g \tan\theta} = \dfrac{F_e \cot\theta}{g}$

Substituting the value of $F_e$:

$m = \dfrac{q^2 \cot\theta}{16\pi\varepsilon_0 g l^2 \sin^2\theta}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle carrying a charge of $2.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ C}$ is positioned directly below the resting bob of a simple pendulum, at a separation of $10 \text{ cm}$. If the mass of the bob is $100 \text{ g}$, determine the charge that must be given to the bob such that the string becomes loose.
questions.solution:
For the string to become loose, the tension in the string must be zero. This happens when the upward electrostatic force balances the downward gravitational force.

$F_{e} = mg$

$\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}} \dfrac{q_{1} q_{2}}{r^2} = mg$

Substituting the given values:

$9 \times 10^9 \times \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-4} \times q_{2}}{(0.1)^2} = 0.1 \times 9.8$

$18 \times 10^7 \times q_{2} = 0.98$

$q_{2} = \dfrac{0.98}{18 \times 10^7} = 5.44 \times 10^{-9} \text{ C}$

The required charge is approximately $5.4 \times 10^{-9} \text{ C}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two particles $A$ and $B$ possessing charges $q$ and $2q$ respectively are located on a smooth table with a separation $d$. A third particle $C$ is to be clamped on the table such that particles $A$ and $B$ remain stationary under electrical forces. Determine the charge on $C$ and its clamping position.
options: $-(6 - 4\sqrt{2})q$, outside $A$ and $B$ at a distance of $(\sqrt{2} + 1)d$ from $A$
$-(6 + 4\sqrt{2})q$, between $A$ and $B$ at a distance of $(\sqrt{2} - 1)d$ from $A$
$-(6 - 4\sqrt{2})q$, between $A$ and $B$ at a distance of $(\sqrt{2} - 1)d$ from $A$
$-(3 - 2\sqrt{2})q$, between $A$ and $B$ at a distance of $(\sqrt{2} - 1)d$ from $A$
questions.solution:
Let the charge of $C$ be $Q$ and its distance from $A$ be $x$. Since $A$ and $B$ have like charges, they repel each other. For them to remain stationary, $C$ must attract both, meaning $C$ must have a negative charge and be placed between $A$ and $B$.

For the equilibrium of particle $A$, the net force on it must be zero:

$\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q(2q)}{d^2} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q|Q|}{x^2}$

$\Rightarrow |Q| = \dfrac{2qx^2}{d^2}$

For the equilibrium of particle $B$, the net force on it must be zero:

$\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q(2q)}{d^2} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{2q|Q|}{(d-x)^2}$

$\Rightarrow |Q| = \dfrac{q(d-x)^2}{d^2}$

Equating the two expressions for $|Q|$:

$2x^2 = (d-x)^2$

Taking the square root on both sides:

$\sqrt{2}x = d - x$

$\Rightarrow x(\sqrt{2} + 1) = d$

$\Rightarrow x = \dfrac{d}{\sqrt{2} + 1} = (\sqrt{2} - 1)d$

Substituting the value of $x$ to find $|Q|$:

$|Q| = \dfrac{2q}{d^2} \left( (\sqrt{2} - 1)d \right)^2$

$\Rightarrow |Q| = 2q (2 + 1 - 2\sqrt{2})$

$\Rightarrow |Q| = (6 - 4\sqrt{2})q$

Since the charge must be negative, $Q = -(6 - 4\sqrt{2})q$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identically charged particles are attached to the opposite ends of a spring having a natural length of $10 \text{ cm}$ and a spring constant of $100 \text{ N m}^{-1}$. The system rests on a smooth horizontal table. Determine the extension in the spring's length if the charge on each particle is $2.0 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C}$. Assume the extension is small compared to the natural length.
questions.solution:
Let the natural length of the spring be $L$ and the extension be $x$.

The electrostatic repulsive force between the two charges is given by Coulomb's law:

$F_{e} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi \epsilon_{0}} \dfrac{q^{2}}{(L+x)^{2}}$

Since the extension $x$ is small compared to the natural length $L$, $L+x \approx L$. Thus,

$F_{e} \approx \dfrac{1}{4\pi \epsilon_{0}} \dfrac{q^{2}}{L^{2}}$

The restoring force of the spring is:

$F_{s} = kx$

In equilibrium, the electrostatic repulsive force is balanced by the restoring force of the spring:

$kx = \dfrac{1}{4\pi \epsilon_{0}} \dfrac{q^{2}}{L^{2}}$

Substituting the given values, $q = 2.0 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C}$, $L = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$, $k = 100 \text{ N m}^{-1}$, and $\dfrac{1}{4\pi \epsilon_{0}} = 9 \times 10^{9} \text{ N m}^{2} \text{ C}^{-2}$:

$100 x = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times (2.0 \times 10^{-8})^{2}}{(0.1)^{2}}$

$100 x = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 4.0 \times 10^{-16}}{0.01}$

$100 x = \dfrac{36 \times 10^{-7}}{0.01}$

$100 x = 36 \times 10^{-5}$

$x = 3.6 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle $A$ with a charge of $2.0 	imes 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ is held fixed on a horizontal table. A second charged particle of mass $80 \text{ g}$ remains in equilibrium on the table at a distance of $10 \text{ cm}$ from the first charge. The coefficient of friction between the table and the second particle is $\mu = 0.2$. Determine the range within which the charge of the second particle may lie.
questions.solution:
The maximum force of static friction acting on the second particle is given by

$f = \mu m g$

Substituting the given values:

$f = 0.2 \times 0.08 \times 9.8 = 0.1568 \text{ N}$

The electrostatic force between the two charges is

$F = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} \dfrac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2}$

Substituting the known values:

$F = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \times |q_2|}{(0.1)^2}$

$F = 1.8 \times 10^6 |q_2|$

For the second particle to remain in equilibrium, the electrostatic force must be less than or equal to the maximum static friction:

$F \le f$

$1.8 \times 10^6 |q_2| \le 0.1568$

$|q_2| \le \dfrac{0.1568}{1.8 \times 10^6}$

$|q_2| \le 8.71 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C}$

Thus, the charge of the second particle must lie between $\pm 8.71 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At the base of a smooth inclined plane with an inclination of $30^\circ$, a particle $A$ having a mass of $100 \text{ g}$ and a charge of $2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ is placed. At what distance from the bottom along the incline should another particle $B$, with the same mass and charge, be positioned so that it remains in equilibrium?
questions.solution:
For particle B to be in equilibrium, the net force acting on it along the inclined plane must be zero.

The downward component of the weight of particle B along the incline is balanced by the upward electrostatic force of repulsion from particle A.

$mg \sin \theta = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q^2}{r^2}$

Substituting the given values $m = 0.1 \text{ kg}$, $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$, $\theta = 30^\circ$, and $q = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$:

$0.1 \times 9.8 \times \sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times (2.0 \times 10^{-6})^2}{r^2}$

$0.1 \times 9.8 \times 0.5 = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-12}}{r^2}$

$0.49 = \dfrac{0.036}{r^2}$

$r^2 = \dfrac{0.036}{0.49} \approx 0.0735 \text{ m}^2$

$r \approx 0.271 \text{ m} = 27.1 \text{ cm}$

The closest value among the options is $27 \text{ cm}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two particles $A$ and $B$, each carrying a charge $Q$, are located a distance $d$ apart. At what point on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ must a particle of charge $q$ be positioned to experience the maximum force, and what is the magnitude of this maximum force?
questions.solution:
Let the two charges $Q$ be placed at $\left(-\dfrac{d}{2}, 0\right)$ and $\left(\dfrac{d}{2}, 0\right)$.

The charge $q$ is placed at $(0, y)$ on the perpendicular bisector.

The net force on $q$ is directed along the y-axis and its magnitude is given by:

$F = 2 \times \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Qq}{\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)^2 + y^2} \cos\theta$

where $\cos\theta = \dfrac{y}{\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)^2 + y^2}}$.

Thus, $F = \dfrac{2Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{y}{\left( \dfrac{d^2}{4} + y^2 \right)^{3/2}}$.

For maximum force, $\dfrac{dF}{dy} = 0$.

$\dfrac{d}{dy} \left[ y \left( \dfrac{d^2}{4} + y^2 \right)^{-3/2} \right] = 0$

$\left( \dfrac{d^2}{4} + y^2 \right)^{-3/2} - \dfrac{3}{2} y \left( \dfrac{d^2}{4} + y^2 \right)^{-5/2} (2y) = 0$

$\dfrac{d^2}{4} + y^2 - 3y^2 = 0 \Rightarrow 2y^2 = \dfrac{d^2}{4} \Rightarrow y = \dfrac{d}{2\sqrt{2}}$.

Substituting $y = \dfrac{d}{2\sqrt{2}}$ into the force equation:

$F_{max} = \dfrac{2Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{\dfrac{d}{2\sqrt{2}}}{\left( \dfrac{d^2}{4} + \dfrac{d^2}{8} \right)^{3/2}}$

$F_{max} = \dfrac{2Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{\dfrac{d}{2\sqrt{2}}}{\left( \dfrac{3d^2}{8} \right)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{2Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{\dfrac{d}{2\sqrt{2}}}{\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}d^3}{16\sqrt{2}}}$

$F_{max} = \dfrac{16Qq}{3\sqrt{3} (4\pi\varepsilon_0 d^2)}$

Since $\dfrac{16}{3\sqrt{3}} \approx \dfrac{16}{5.196} \approx 3.08$, we get:

$F_{max} \approx \dfrac{3.08 Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 d^2}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two particles $A$ and $B$, each carrying a charge $Q$, are held fixed with a separation $d$ between them. A particle $C$ having mass $m$ and charge $q$ is kept at the midpoint of the line segment $AB$. If particle $C$ is displaced through a distance $x$ perpendicular to $AB$, determine the electric force experienced by it.
questions.solution:
Let the positions of particles $A$ and $B$ be at a distance $\dfrac{d}{2}$ from the origin on the line connecting them. Particle $C$ is displaced by a distance $x$ along the perpendicular bisector.

The distance of particle $C$ from both $A$ and $B$ is $r = \sqrt{x^2 + \dfrac{d^2}{4}}$.

The magnitude of the electric force exerted by each charge $Q$ on $q$ is $F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Qq}{r^2}$.

By symmetry, the components of the forces parallel to the line $AB$ are equal and opposite, thus cancelling each other out.

The components of the forces perpendicular to $AB$ (along the displacement direction) add up. The net force is $F_{net} = 2F \cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the force vector and the perpendicular bisector.

From the geometry, $\cos\theta = \dfrac{x}{r} = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + \dfrac{d^2}{4}}}$.

Substituting $F$ and $\cos\theta$ into the net force equation:

$F_{net} = 2 \left( \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Qq}{x^2 + \dfrac{d^2}{4}} \right) \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + \dfrac{d^2}{4}}}$

$F_{net} = \dfrac{Qqx}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 \left(x^2 + \dfrac{d^2}{4}\right)^{3/2}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two particles $A$ and $B$, each carrying a charge $Q$, are held fixed with a separation $d$ between them. A particle $C$ having mass $m$ and charge $q$ is kept at the midpoint of the line segment $AB$. Particle $C$ is displaced through a distance $x$ perpendicular to $AB$. Assuming $x \ll d$, which of the following expressions represents the approximate electric force experienced by it?
questions.solution:
Let the positions of particles $A$ and $B$ be $(-\dfrac{d}{2}, 0)$ and $(\dfrac{d}{2}, 0)$ respectively. The initial position of particle $C$ is $(0, 0)$.

When $C$ is displaced by a distance $x$ perpendicular to $AB$, its new position is $(0, x)$.

The distance of particle $C$ from both $A$ and $B$ is $r = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)^2 + x^2}$.

The magnitude of the electric force exerted by each charge $Q$ on $q$ is:

$F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Qq}{r^2}$

By symmetry, the components of the forces parallel to the line $AB$ cancel each other out. The net force is directed along the perpendicular bisector.

$F_{net} = 2F \cos\theta$

From the geometry of the figure, $\cos\theta = \dfrac{x}{r}$.

Substituting the values of $F$ and $\cos\theta$:

$F_{net} = 2 \left( \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Qq}{r^2} \right) \left( \dfrac{x}{r} \right) = \dfrac{2Qqx}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^3} = \dfrac{Qqx}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 \left( \left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)^2 + x^2 \right)^{3/2}}$

Since it is given that $x \ll d$, we can approximate $\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)^2 + x^2 \approx \left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)^2$.

$F_{net} \approx \dfrac{Qqx}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 \left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)^3} = \dfrac{Qqx}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 \left(\dfrac{d^3}{8}\right)}$

$F_{net} = \dfrac{4Qqx}{\pi\varepsilon_0 d^3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two particles $A$ and $B$, each carrying a charge $Q$, are held fixed with a separation $d$ between them. A particle $C$ having mass $m$ and charge $q$ is kept at the midpoint of the line segment $AB$. Particle $C$ is displaced through a small distance $x$ ($x \ll d$) perpendicular to $AB$ and then released. Assuming $Q$ and $q$ possess opposite signs such that the particle executes simple harmonic motion, find the time period of the oscillations.
questions.solution:
Let the charges $Q$ be placed at $(-d/2, 0)$ and $(d/2, 0)$.

The particle $C$ is displaced to $(0, x)$ along the perpendicular bisector.

The distance of $C$ from each charge $Q$ is $r = \sqrt{(d/2)^2 + x^2}$.

The attractive electrostatic force between $C$ and each charge $Q$ is $F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Qq}{r^2}$.

The components of the forces parallel to $AB$ cancel each other, while the components perpendicular to $AB$ add up to provide the restoring force.

The net restoring force is $F_{net} = 2F \cos\theta$, where $\cos\theta = \dfrac{x}{r}$.

$F_{net} = 2 \left( \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Qq}{r^2} \right) \left( \dfrac{x}{r} \right) = \dfrac{2Qqx}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^3}$

Since $x \ll d$, $r \approx \dfrac{d}{2}$.

$F_{net} = \dfrac{2Qqx}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 (d/2)^3} = \dfrac{16Qqx}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 d^3} = \dfrac{4Qq}{\pi\varepsilon_0 d^3} x$

The restoring force is proportional to $x$, so the motion is simple harmonic with force constant $k = \dfrac{4Qq}{\pi\varepsilon_0 d^3}$.

The time period of oscillation is $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m \pi\varepsilon_0 d^3}{4Qq}} = \left(\dfrac{m\pi^3 \varepsilon_0 d^3}{Qq}\right)^{1/2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two particles $A$ and $B$, each carrying a charge $Q$, are held fixed with a separation $d$ between them. A particle $C$ having mass $m$ and charge $q$ is kept at the midpoint of the line $AB$. If the particle $C$ is displaced by a distance $x$ along the line $AB$, determine the magnitude of the electric force experienced by it.
questions.solution:
Let the positions of particles $A$ and $B$ be at $-\dfrac{d}{2}$ and $\dfrac{d}{2}$ respectively, with the origin at the midpoint.

When particle $C$ is displaced by a distance $x$ towards $B$, its new distance from $A$ is $\dfrac{d}{2} + x$ and from $B$ is $\dfrac{d}{2} - x$.

The electric force on $C$ due to $A$ is $F_A = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Q q}{\left(\dfrac{d}{2} + x\right)^2}$ directed towards $B$.

The electric force on $C$ due to $B$ is $F_B = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Q q}{\left(\dfrac{d}{2} - x\right)^2}$ directed towards $A$.

The net electric force experienced by $C$ is the difference between these two forces:

$F = F_B - F_A = \dfrac{Q q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \left[ \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{d}{2} - x\right)^2} - \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{d}{2} + x\right)^2} \right]$

$F = \dfrac{Q q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \left[ \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{d}{2} + x\right)^2 - \left(\dfrac{d}{2} - x\right)^2}{\left(\dfrac{d^2}{4} - x^2\right)^2} \right]$

Using the identity $(a+b)^2 - (a-b)^2 = 4ab$, the numerator becomes $4 \left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right) x = 2dx$.

$F = \dfrac{Q q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \left[ \dfrac{2dx}{\left(\dfrac{d^2}{4} - x^2\right)^2} \right]$

$F = \dfrac{Q q d x}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 \left(\dfrac{d^2}{4} - x^2\right)^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two particles $A$ and $B$, each carrying a charge $Q$, are held fixed with a separation $d$ between them. A particle $C$ having mass $m$ and charge $q$ is kept at the midpoint of the line $AB$ and is then displaced by a distance $x$ along the line $AB$. Assuming $x \ll d$, determine the approximate magnitude of the electric force experienced by particle $C$.
questions.solution:
Let the charges $A$ and $B$ be located at $x = -\dfrac{d}{2}$ and $x = \dfrac{d}{2}$ respectively.

The particle $C$ is displaced to a position $x$ from the origin (midpoint of $AB$).

The electric force on $C$ due to $A$ is $F_A = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Q q}{(\dfrac{d}{2} + x)^2}$ directed towards $B$.

The electric force on $C$ due to $B$ is $F_B = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Q q}{(\dfrac{d}{2} - x)^2}$ directed towards $A$.

The net force on $C$ is $F = F_B - F_A$ (towards $A$):

$F = \dfrac{Q q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \left[ \dfrac{1}{(\dfrac{d}{2} - x)^2} - \dfrac{1}{(\dfrac{d}{2} + x)^2} \right]$

$F = \dfrac{Q q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \left[ \dfrac{(\dfrac{d}{2} + x)^2 - (\dfrac{d}{2} - x)^2}{(\dfrac{d^2}{4} - x^2)^2} \right]$

$F = \dfrac{Q q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \left[ \dfrac{2 d x}{(\dfrac{d^2}{4} - x^2)^2} \right]$

Since $x \ll d$, we can neglect $x^2$ in the denominator, so $(\dfrac{d^2}{4} - x^2)^2 \approx \dfrac{d^4}{16}$.

$F \approx \dfrac{Q q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \left( \dfrac{2 d x}{\dfrac{d^4}{16}} \right)$

$F \approx \dfrac{Q q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \left( \dfrac{32 x}{d^3} \right)$

$F \approx \dfrac{8 Q q x}{\pi\varepsilon_0 d^3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two particles $A$ and $B$, each carrying a charge $Q$, are held fixed with a separation $d$ between them. A particle $C$ having mass $m$ and charge $q$ is kept at the midpoint of the line $AB$. The particle $C$ is displaced by a small distance $x \ll d$ along the line $AB$ and released. Assuming the charges $Q$ and $q$ have the same sign so that particle $C$ executes simple harmonic motion, determine the time period of the oscillations.
questions.solution:
Let the origin be at the midpoint of the line joining $A$ and $B$. The coordinates of $A$ and $B$ are $-d/2$ and $d/2$.

When particle $C$ is displaced by a small distance $x$ towards $B$, its distance from $A$ becomes $d/2 + x$ and from $B$ becomes $d/2 - x$.

The net force on $C$ is:

$F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi \varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Qq}{(d/2 + x)^2} - \dfrac{1}{4\pi \varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Qq}{(d/2 - x)^2}$

$F = \dfrac{Qq}{4\pi \varepsilon_0} \left[ \dfrac{(d/2 - x)^2 - (d/2 + x)^2}{(d^2/4 - x^2)^2} \right]$

$F = \dfrac{Qq}{4\pi \varepsilon_0} \left[ \dfrac{-2dx}{(d^2/4 - x^2)^2} \right]$

Since $x \ll d$, the term $x^2$ can be neglected in the denominator:

$F \approx \dfrac{Qq}{4\pi \varepsilon_0} \left[ \dfrac{-2dx}{(d^2/4)^2} \right] = -\dfrac{8Qq}{\pi \varepsilon_0 d^3} x$

Comparing this with the standard equation of simple harmonic motion $F = -Kx$, the effective force constant is $K = \dfrac{8Qq}{\pi \varepsilon_0 d^3}$.

The time period of oscillation is given by:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{K}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{\pi \varepsilon_0 m d^3}{8Qq}}$

$T = \left( \dfrac{4\pi^2 \pi \varepsilon_0 m d^3}{8Qq} \right)^{1/2} = \left( \dfrac{\pi^3 \varepsilon_0 m d^3}{2Qq} \right)^{1/2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charge of $1.0 	imes 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ experiences an electric force of $1.5 	imes 10^{-3} \text{ N}$. Determine the magnitude of the electric field at the location of the charge.
questions.solution:
The relation between electric force $F$, charge $q$, and electric field $E$ is given by $F = qE$.

Rearranging for the electric field $E$ gives $E = \dfrac{F}{q}$.

Substituting the given values:

$E = \dfrac{1.5 \times 10^{-3}}{1.0 \times 10^{-6}}$

$E = 1.5 \times 10^{3} \text{ N/C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two particles $A$ and $B$, possessing charges of $+2.00 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ and $-4.00 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ respectively, are held fixed at a separation of $20.0 \text{ cm}$. Find the point(s) on the line $AB$ at which the electric field is zero.
questions.solution:
Let the point where the electric field is zero be at a distance $x$ from charge $A$.

Since the charges have opposite signs, the null point must lie outside the line segment joining the two charges, on the side of the charge with the smaller magnitude. Here, $|q_A| < |q_B|$, so the point lies on the side of $A$, which corresponds to the direction along $BA$.

At the null point, the magnitudes of the electric fields due to both charges must be equal:

$\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{|q_A|}{x^2} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{|q_B|}{(x + d)^2}$

Substituting the given values:

$\dfrac{2.00 \times 10^{-6}}{x^2} = \dfrac{4.00 \times 10^{-6}}{(x + 20.0)^2}$

$\dfrac{1}{x^2} = \dfrac{2}{(x + 20.0)^2}$

Taking the square root of both sides:

$\dfrac{1}{x} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{x + 20.0}$

$x + 20.0 = \sqrt{2}x$

$x(\sqrt{2} - 1) = 20.0$

$x = \dfrac{20.0}{\sqrt{2} - 1}$

Rationalizing the denominator:

$x = 20.0(\sqrt{2} + 1)$

Using $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$:

$x = 20.0(1.414 + 1) = 20.0 \times 2.414 = 48.28 \text{ cm}$

Rounding off to three significant figures, the distance is $48.3 \text{ cm}$.

Thus, the electric field is zero at a distance of $48.3 \text{ cm}$ from $A$ along $BA$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two particles $A$ and $B$, possessing charges of $+2.00 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ and $-4.00 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ respectively, are held fixed at a separation of $20.0 \text{ cm}$. Find the point(s) on the line $AB$ at which the electric potential is zero.
questions.solution:
Let $A$ be at the origin and $B$ be at a distance of $20 \text{ cm}$ from $A$.

The electric potential at a point $P$ is given by $V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \left( \dfrac{q_A}{r_A} + \dfrac{q_B}{r_B} \right)$.

For $V = 0$, we have $\dfrac{q_A}{r_A} = -\dfrac{q_B}{r_B}$.

Substituting the given charges:

$\dfrac{2.00 \times 10^{-6}}{r_A} = \dfrac{4.00 \times 10^{-6}}{r_B} \Rightarrow r_B = 2r_A$

Case 1: $P$ lies between $A$ and $B$.

$r_A + r_B = 20$

$r_A + 2r_A = 20 \Rightarrow 3r_A = 20 \Rightarrow r_A = \dfrac{20}{3} \text{ cm}$

This point is $\dfrac{20}{3} \text{ cm}$ from $A$ along $AB$.

Case 2: $P$ lies outside the segment $AB$. Since $|q_A| < |q_B|$, the point must be closer to $A$, meaning it lies on the side of $A$ along the extended line $BA$.

$r_B - r_A = 20$

$2r_A - r_A = 20 \Rightarrow r_A = 20 \text{ cm}$

This point is $20 \text{ cm}$ from $A$ along $BA$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At a distance of $40 \text{ cm}$ from a point charge, the electric field has a magnitude of $5.0 \text{ N C}^{-1}$. Determine the magnitude of the charge.
questions.solution:
The electric field due to a point charge $q$ at a distance $r$ is given by $E = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} \dfrac{q}{r^2}$.

Given $E = 5.0 \text{ N C}^{-1}$ and $r = 40 \text{ cm} = 0.4 \text{ m}$.

Substituting the values:

$5.0 = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times q}{(0.4)^2}$

$q = \dfrac{5.0 \times 0.16}{9 \times 10^9}$

$q = \dfrac{0.8}{9 \times 10^9}$

$q = 8.88 \times 10^{-11} \text{ C} \approx 8.9 \times 10^{-11} \text{ C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A water particle with a mass of $10.0 \text{ mg}$ and a charge of $1.50 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ remains suspended in a room. Determine the magnitude and direction of the electric field in the room.
questions.solution:
For the water particle to remain suspended, the upward electric force must balance the downward gravitational force.

$qE = mg$

$E = \dfrac{mg}{q}$

Substituting the given values, $m = 10.0 \text{ mg} = 10.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ kg}$, $q = 1.50 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$, and $g = 9.8 \text{ m s}^{-2}$:

$E = \dfrac{10.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 9.8}{1.50 \times 10^{-6}}$

$E = \dfrac{98}{1.50} = 65.3 \text{ N C}^{-1}$

Since the charge is positive, the electric field must be directed upward to exert an upward force.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three identical charges, each with a value of $1.0 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C}$, are situated at the corners of an equilateral triangle having a side length of $20 \text{ cm}$. Determine the electric field and potential at the centre of the triangle.
questions.solution:
Due to the symmetry of the equilateral triangle, the electric field vectors at the centroid due to the three identical charges are equal in magnitude and separated by an angle of $120^{\circ}$. Their vector sum is zero. Thus, the net electric field at the centre is zero.

The distance $r$ from any corner to the centroid of an equilateral triangle of side $a$ is given by $r = \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{3}}$.

Given $a = 20 \text{ cm} = 0.2 \text{ m}$, we have $r = \dfrac{0.2}{\sqrt{3}} \text{ m}$.

The electric potential is a scalar quantity. The net potential at the centre is the sum of the potentials due to the three charges:

$V = 3 \times \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{q}{r}$

Substituting the given values:

$V = 3 \times \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 1.0 \times 10^{-8}}{\dfrac{0.2}{\sqrt{3}}}$

$V = \dfrac{270 \sqrt{3}}{0.2} = 1350 \sqrt{3}$

Using $\sqrt{3} \approx 1.732$:

$V \approx 1350 \times 1.732 \approx 2338 \text{ V} \approx 2.3 \times 10^3 \text{ V}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A positive charge $Q$ is distributed uniformly over a circular ring of radius $R$. A particle having a mass $m$ and a negative charge $q$ is placed on its axis at a distance $x$ from the centre. Determine the force on the particle. Assuming $x \ll R$, find the time period of oscillation of the particle if it is released from this position.
options: Force: $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Qqx}{(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}}$ away from the centre; Time period: $\left(\dfrac{8 \pi^3 \varepsilon_0 m R^3}{Qq}\right)^{1/2}$
Force: $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Qqx}{(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}}$ away from the centre; Time period: $\left(\dfrac{16 \pi^3 \varepsilon_0 m R^3}{Qq}\right)^{1/2}$
Force: $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Qqx}{(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}}$ towards the centre; Time period: $\left(\dfrac{8 \pi^3 \varepsilon_0 m R^3}{Qq}\right)^{1/2}$
Force: $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Qqx}{(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}}$ towards the centre; Time period: $\left(\dfrac{16 \pi^3 \varepsilon_0 m R^3}{Qq}\right)^{1/2}$
questions.solution:
The electric field at a distance $x$ on the axis of a uniformly charged ring of radius $R$ and charge $Q$ is given by:

$E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Qx}{(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}}$

The force on a particle of negative charge $q$ is:

$F = qE = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Qqx}{(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}}$

Since the charge on the particle is negative and the ring is positively charged, the force is attractive and directed towards the centre of the ring.

For $x \ll R$, we can approximate $(R^2+x^2)^{3/2} \approx R^3$. The restoring force becomes:

$F = \left(\dfrac{Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R^3}\right) x$

This represents simple harmonic motion with force constant $k = \dfrac{Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R^3}$.

The time period of oscillation is:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{4\pi\varepsilon_0 m R^3}{Qq}} = \left(\dfrac{16 \pi^3 \varepsilon_0 m R^3}{Qq}\right)^{1/2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A rod of length $L$ carries a total charge $Q$ distributed uniformly along its length. The rod is bent into the shape of a semicircle. Determine the magnitude of the electric field at the centre of curvature of the semicircle.
questions.solution:
Let the radius of the semicircle be $R$. Since the rod of length $L$ is bent into a semicircle, the length of the arc is equal to $L$.

$\pi R = L \Rightarrow R = \dfrac{L}{\pi}$

The linear charge density of the rod is $\lambda = \dfrac{Q}{L}$.

Consider a small element of the semicircle subtending an angle $d\theta$ at the centre. The charge on this element is $dq = \lambda R d\theta$.

The electric field due to this element at the centre is $dE = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{dq}{R^2} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{\lambda R d\theta}{R^2} = \dfrac{\lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R} d\theta$.

By symmetry, the components of the electric field perpendicular to the angle bisector cancel out. The net electric field is along the angle bisector.

$E = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} dE \cos\theta = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R} \cos\theta d\theta$

$E = \dfrac{\lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R} [\sin\theta]_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} = \dfrac{\lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R} (1 - (-1)) = \dfrac{2\lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R} = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 R}$

Substituting $\lambda = \dfrac{Q}{L}$ and $R = \dfrac{L}{\pi}$ into the expression for $E$:

$E = \dfrac{Q/L}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 (L/\pi)} = \dfrac{Q \pi}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 L^2} = \dfrac{Q}{2\varepsilon_0 L^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A rod of length $10 \text{ cm}$ carries a charge of $+50 \mu\text{C}$ uniformly distributed along its length. Determine the magnitude of the electric field at a point located $10 \text{ cm}$ from both ends of the rod.
questions.solution:
Length of the rod, $L = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$

Charge on the rod, $Q = 50 \mu\text{C} = 50 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$

Linear charge density, $\lambda = \dfrac{Q}{L} = \dfrac{50 \times 10^{-6}}{0.1} = 5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ C/m}$

The point is at a distance of $10 \text{ cm}$ from both ends of the rod. Thus, the point and the two ends of the rod form an equilateral triangle of side $10 \text{ cm}$. The point lies on the perpendicular bisector of the rod.

The perpendicular distance of the point from the rod is $r = \sqrt{10^2 - 5^2} = 5\sqrt{3} \text{ cm} = 5\sqrt{3} \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$.

The angle subtended by each half of the rod at the point is $\theta_1 = \theta_2 = 30^\circ$.

The electric field at the point is given by:

$E = \dfrac{k \lambda}{r} (\sin \theta_1 + \sin \theta_2)$

Substituting the values:

$E = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 5 \times 10^{-4}}{5\sqrt{3} \times 10^{-2}} (\sin 30^\circ + \sin 30^\circ)$

$E = \dfrac{45 \times 10^5}{5\sqrt{3} \times 10^{-2}} \times 1$

$E = \dfrac{9 \times 10^7}{\sqrt{3}} = 3\sqrt{3} \times 10^7 \text{ N/C}$

$E \approx 3 \times 1.732 \times 10^7 \text{ N/C} = 5.196 \times 10^7 \text{ N/C} \approx 5.2 \times 10^7 \text{ N/C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: For a uniformly charged ring of radius $R$, determine the distance from its centre along the axis where the electric field achieves its maximum value.
questions.solution:
The electric field at a distance $x$ from the centre of a uniformly charged ring of radius $R$ and charge $Q$ on its axis is given by

$E = \dfrac{kQx}{(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$

For the electric field to be maximum, $\dfrac{dE}{dx} = 0$

$\dfrac{d}{dx} \left[ \dfrac{x}{(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}} \right] = 0$

$\dfrac{(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2} \cdot 1 - x \cdot \dfrac{3}{2}(R^2 + x^2)^{1/2} \cdot 2x}{(R^2 + x^2)^3} = 0$

$(R^2 + x^2)^{1/2} [R^2 + x^2 - 3x^2] = 0$

$R^2 - 2x^2 = 0$

$x = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire is shaped into a regular hexagon, and a total charge $q$ is uniformly distributed along it. Determine the electric field at the centre. You can answer this without performing any numerical calculations.
options: $\dfrac{6q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 a^2}$, where $a$ is the side length
$\dfrac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 a^2}$, where $a$ is the side length
$\dfrac{\sqrt{3}q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 a^2}$, where $a$ is the side length
questions.solution:
A regular hexagon is a highly symmetric geometric figure.

Since the charge $q$ is uniformly distributed along the wire, each of the six sides of the hexagon has the same linear charge density and produces an electric field of equal magnitude at the centre.

For every side of the hexagon, there is an identical side directly opposite to it. The electric field vectors produced by any pair of opposite sides at the centre are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction.

Thus, the electric fields from all pairs of opposite sides cancel each other out completely.

Therefore, the net electric field at the centre of the regular hexagon is zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A circular wire-loop of radius $a$ carries a total charge $Q$ uniformly distributed over its length. A small segment of length $dL$ is cut off from the wire. Determine the electric field at the centre due to the remaining wire.
questions.solution:
The electric field at the centre of a complete uniformly charged circular loop is zero.

By the principle of superposition, the electric field due to the remaining wire is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the electric field due to the small cut-off segment.

The linear charge density of the wire is $\lambda = \dfrac{Q}{2\pi a}$.

The charge on the small segment of length $dL$ is $dq = \lambda dL = \dfrac{QdL}{2\pi a}$.

Treating this small segment as a point charge, the magnitude of the electric field at the centre due to it is $E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi \varepsilon_0} \dfrac{dq}{a^2}$.

Substituting the value of $dq$, we get $E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi \varepsilon_0} \dfrac{\dfrac{QdL}{2\pi a}}{a^2} = \dfrac{QdL}{8\pi^2 \varepsilon_0 a^3}$.

Thus, the electric field at the centre due to the remaining wire is $\dfrac{QdL}{8\pi^2 \varepsilon_0 a^3}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A positive charge $q$ is situated at a distance $d$ from the centre of a solid conducting cube. Determine the electric field at the centre of the cube produced by the charges appearing on its surface.
options: $\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 d^2}$ directed away from the charge $q$
questions.solution:
The net electric field inside a solid conducting cube under electrostatic conditions is zero.

The total electric field at the centre of the cube is the vector sum of the electric field due to the external point charge $q$ and the electric field due to the induced charges on the surface of the cube.

$\vec{E}_{\text{net}} = \vec{E}_{q} + \vec{E}_{\text{induced}} = 0$

$\Rightarrow \vec{E}_{\text{induced}} = -\vec{E}_{q}$

The electric field at the centre of the cube due to the positive point charge $q$ at a distance $d$ is given by:

$|\vec{E}_{q}| = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 d^2}$

Since $q$ is a positive charge, $\vec{E}_{q}$ is directed away from the charge $q$.

Therefore, the electric field due to the induced charges on the surface of the cube must have the same magnitude but opposite direction to cancel $\vec{E}_{q}$.

$|\vec{E}_{\text{induced}}| = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 d^2}$

The direction of $\vec{E}_{\text{induced}}$ is towards the charge $q$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A pendulum bob having a mass of $80 \text{ mg}$ and carrying a charge of $2 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C}$ remains at rest in a uniform horizontal electric field of $20 \text{ kV m}^{-1}$. Determine the tension in the thread.
questions.solution:
Given, mass of the bob, $m = 80 \text{ mg} = 80 \times 10^{-6} \text{ kg}$

Charge on the bob, $q = 2 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C}$

Electric field, $E = 20 \text{ kV m}^{-1} = 2 \times 10^{4} \text{ V m}^{-1}$

The electric force acting on the bob horizontally is:

$F_{e} = qE = (2 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C})(2 \times 10^{4} \text{ V m}^{-1}) = 4 \times 10^{-4} \text{ N}$

The gravitational force acting on the bob vertically downwards is:

$W = mg = (80 \times 10^{-6} \text{ kg})(9.8 \text{ m s}^{-2}) = 7.84 \times 10^{-4} \text{ N}$

Since the bob is at rest, the tension $T$ in the thread balances the resultant of the electric force and the weight. Since $F_{e}$ and $W$ are perpendicular to each other, the tension is given by:

$T = \sqrt{F_{e}^2 + W^2}$

Substituting the values:

$T = \sqrt{(4 \times 10^{-4})^2 + (7.84 \times 10^{-4})^2}$

$T = 10^{-4} \sqrt{16 + 61.4656}$

$T = 10^{-4} \sqrt{77.4656}$

$T \approx 8.8 \times 10^{-4} \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle having mass $m$ and charge $q$ is projected with a speed $u$ against a uniform electric field $E$. Determine the distance it will cover before coming to momentary rest.
questions.solution:
The force acting on the particle due to the uniform electric field is $F = qE$.

The retardation of the particle is $a = \dfrac{F}{m} = \dfrac{qE}{m}$.

Using the third equation of kinematics, $v^2 = u^2 - 2as$.

Since the particle comes to momentary rest, its final velocity $v = 0$.

Substituting the values, $0 = u^2 - 2 \left(\dfrac{qE}{m}\right) s$.

Solving for the distance $s$, we get $s = \dfrac{mu^2}{2qE}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle with a mass of $1 \text{ g}$ and a charge of $2.5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ C}$ is released from rest within an electric field of $1.2 \times 10^4 \text{ N C}^{-1}$. Determine the respective magnitudes of the electric force and the gravitational force acting on this particle.
questions.solution:
Given, mass of the particle $m = 1 \text{ g} = 10^{-3} \text{ kg}$

Charge of the particle $q = 2.5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ C}$

Electric field $E = 1.2 \times 10^4 \text{ N C}^{-1}$

The magnitude of the electric force is given by $F_e = qE$

$F_e = (2.5 \times 10^{-4}) \times (1.2 \times 10^4) = 3.0 \text{ N}$

The magnitude of the gravitational force is given by $F_g = mg$

$F_g = (10^{-3}) \times 9.8 = 9.8 \times 10^{-3} \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle with a mass of $1 \text{ g}$ and a charge of $2.5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ C}$ is released from rest within an electric field of $1.2 \times 10^4 \text{ N C}^{-1}$. Determine the time it will take for the particle to cover a distance of $40 \text{ cm}$.
questions.solution:
The force experienced by the particle in the electric field is given by:

$F = qE$

Substituting the given values:

$F = (2.5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ C}) \times (1.2 \times 10^4 \text{ N C}^{-1}) = 3.0 \text{ N}$

The acceleration of the particle is:

$a = \dfrac{F}{m} = \dfrac{3.0 \text{ N}}{10^{-3} \text{ kg}} = 3000 \text{ m s}^{-2}$

Using the second equation of motion for a particle starting from rest ($u = 0$):

$s = \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$

Substituting $s = 40 \text{ cm} = 0.4 \text{ m}$:

$0.4 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 3000 \times t^2$

$t^2 = \dfrac{0.8}{3000} = \dfrac{8}{3} \times 10^{-4} \text{ s}^2$

$t = \sqrt{\dfrac{8}{3}} \times 10^{-2} \text{ s} \approx 1.63 \times 10^{-2} \text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle with a mass of $1 \text{ g}$ and a charge of $2.5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ C}$ is released from rest within an electric field of $1.2 \times 10^4 \text{ N C}^{-1}$. Determine the speed of the particle after it has travelled a distance of $40 \text{ cm}$.
questions.solution:
Given, mass of the particle, $m = 1 \text{ g} = 10^{-3} \text{ kg}$

Charge, $q = 2.5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ C}$

Electric field, $E = 1.2 \times 10^4 \text{ N C}^{-1}$

Distance travelled, $s = 40 \text{ cm} = 0.4 \text{ m}$

The force experienced by the particle in the electric field is:

$F = qE = (2.5 \times 10^{-4}) \times (1.2 \times 10^4) = 3.0 \text{ N}$

The acceleration of the particle is:

$a = \dfrac{F}{m} = \dfrac{3.0}{10^{-3}} = 3000 \text{ m s}^{-2}$

Using the equation of motion $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with initial velocity $u = 0$:

$v^2 = 0 + 2 \times 3000 \times 0.4 = 2400$

$v = \sqrt{2400} = 20\sqrt{6} \approx 48.99 \text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 49.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle with a mass of $1 \text{ g}$ and a charge of $2.5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ C}$ is released from rest within an electric field of $1.2 \times 10^4 \text{ N C}^{-1}$. Compute the work done by the electric force on the particle as it travels a distance of $40 \text{ cm}$.
questions.solution:
The electric force acting on the particle is given by $F = qE$.

Since the particle is released from rest, it moves in the direction of the electric field. The work done by the electric force as the particle travels a distance $d$ is $W = Fd = qEd$.

Substituting the given values:

$W = (2.5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ C}) \times (1.2 \times 10^4 \text{ N C}^{-1}) \times (0.4 \text{ m})$

$W = 3.0 \text{ N} \times 0.4 \text{ m} = 1.20 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball having a mass of $100 \text{ g}$ and a charge of $4.9 \times 10^{-5} \text{ C}$ is released from rest into an area containing a horizontal electric field of $2.0 \times 10^4 \text{ N C}^{-1}$. Describe the path taken by the ball.
options: A straight line along the resultant force
questions.solution:
The forces acting on the ball are the gravitational force acting downwards and the electric force acting horizontally.

Gravitational force is $F_g = mg = 0.1 \times 9.8 = 0.98 \text{ N}$.

Electric force is $F_e = qE = 4.9 \times 10^{-5} \times 2.0 \times 10^4 = 0.98 \text{ N}$.

Both forces are constant in magnitude and direction, so their resultant force is also a constant vector.

Since the ball is released from rest, its initial velocity is zero. Under the action of a constant resultant force with zero initial velocity, the acceleration is constant and the particle moves in a straight line along the direction of the resultant force.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball having a mass of $100 \text{ g}$ and a charge of $4.9 \times 10^{-5} \text{ C}$ is released from rest into an area containing a horizontal electric field of $2.0 \times 10^4 \text{ N C}^{-1}$. Determine the resultant force acting on the ball.
options: $0.98 \text{ N}$ making an angle of $45^\circ$ with the horizontal
$1.4 \text{ N}$ making an angle of $45^\circ$ with the horizontal
$2.0 \text{ N}$ making an angle of $45^\circ$ with the horizontal
$1.4 \text{ N}$ making an angle of $30^\circ$ with the horizontal
questions.solution:
Mass of the ball, $m = 100 \text{ g} = 0.1 \text{ kg}$

Charge on the ball, $q = 4.9 \times 10^{-5} \text{ C}$

Electric field, $E = 2.0 \times 10^4 \text{ N C}^{-1}$

The gravitational force acting on the ball is vertically downwards:

$F_g = mg = 0.1 \times 9.8 = 0.98 \text{ N}$

The electric force acting on the ball is horizontal:

$F_e = qE = 4.9 \times 10^{-5} \times 2.0 \times 10^4 = 0.98 \text{ N}$

Since $F_g$ and $F_e$ are perpendicular to each other, the magnitude of the resultant force is:

$F = \sqrt{F_g^2 + F_e^2} = \sqrt{(0.98)^2 + (0.98)^2} = 0.98\sqrt{2} \approx 1.386 \text{ N} \approx 1.4 \text{ N}$

The angle $\theta$ made by the resultant force with the horizontal is given by:

$\tan \theta = \dfrac{F_g}{F_e} = \dfrac{0.98}{0.98} = 1$

$\theta = 45^\circ$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball having a mass of $100 \text{ g}$ and a charge of $4.9 \times 10^{-5} \text{ C}$ is released from rest into an area containing a horizontal electric field of $2.0 \times 10^4 \text{ N C}^{-1}$. Where will the ball be located after $2 \text{ s}$?
options: $28 \text{ m}$ from the starting point along its line of motion
$14 \text{ m}$ from the starting point along its line of motion
$20 \text{ m}$ from the starting point along its line of motion
$56 \text{ m}$ from the starting point along its line of motion
questions.solution:
Horizontal force acting on the ball:

$F_x = qE = (4.9 \times 10^{-5}) \times (2.0 \times 10^4) = 0.98 \text{ N}$

Vertical force acting on the ball (taking $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$):

$F_y = mg = 0.1 \times 10 = 1 \text{ N}$

Net force acting on the ball:

$F = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2} = \sqrt{(0.98)^2 + (1)^2} = \sqrt{0.9604 + 1} = \sqrt{1.9604} \approx 1.4 \text{ N}$

Acceleration of the ball:

$a = \dfrac{F}{m} = \dfrac{1.4}{0.1} = 14 \text{ m s}^{-2}$

Distance traveled in $t = 2 \text{ s}$:

$s = \dfrac{1}{2}at^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 14 \times (2)^2 = 28 \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The bob of a simple pendulum possesses a mass of $40 \text{ g}$ and a positive charge of $4.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$. It completes $20$ oscillations in $45 \text{ s}$. A vertical electric field of magnitude $2.5 \times 10^4 \text{ N C}^{-1}$ pointing upward is subsequently switched on. Determine the time it will now require to execute $20$ oscillations.
questions.solution:
