The initial time period of the simple pendulum is given by $T_1 = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$.

When the vertical upward electric field is switched on, the electric force acts upwards. The net downward acceleration of the bob becomes $g_{eff} = g - \dfrac{qE}{m}$.

Given $m = 40 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg}$, $q = 4.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$, $E = 2.5 \times 10^4 \text{ N C}^{-1}$, and taking $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$:

$\dfrac{qE}{m} = \dfrac{4.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 2.5 \times 10^4}{40 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{0.1}{0.04} = 2.5 \text{ m s}^{-2}$

$g_{eff} = 10 - 2.5 = 7.5 \text{ m s}^{-2}$

The new time period is $T_2 = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g_{eff}}}$.

The ratio of the time taken for $20$ oscillations is equal to the ratio of their time periods:

$\dfrac{t_2}{t_1} = \dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{g}{g_{eff}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{10}{7.5}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{4}{3}} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$

Substituting $t_1 = 45 \text{ s}$:

$t_2 = 45 \times \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} = 30\sqrt{3} \approx 30 \times 1.732 = 51.96 \text{ s}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, we get $t_2 \approx 52 \text{ s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Resting on a smooth horizontal table, a block of mass $m$ with a charge $q$ is connected to a wall by an unstressed spring having a spring constant $k$, as illustrated in the figure. Subsequently, a horizontal electric field $E$ is switched on parallel to the spring. Determine the amplitude of the resulting simple harmonic motion of the block.
questions.solution:
When the horizontal electric field $E$ is switched on, a constant electric force $F = qE$ acts on the block.

This constant force shifts the equilibrium (mean) position of the spring-mass system.

Let the new equilibrium position be at a distance $x_0$ from the initial unstretched position. At equilibrium, the spring force balances the electric force:

$k x_0 = qE \Rightarrow x_0 = \dfrac{qE}{k}$

Initially, the block is at rest at the unstretched position ($x = 0$). Since its velocity is zero at this point, it acts as an extreme position for the resulting simple harmonic motion.

The amplitude $A$ of the oscillation is the distance between the mean position and the extreme position:

$A = |x_0 - 0| = \dfrac{qE}{k}$

Alternatively, applying the work-energy theorem between the initial position and the position of maximum extension $x_{max}$ (where velocity is again zero):

$qE x_{max} = \dfrac{1}{2} k x_{max}^2 \Rightarrow x_{max} = \dfrac{2qE}{k}$

The amplitude is half of the maximum displacement:

$A = \dfrac{x_{max}}{2} = \dfrac{qE}{k}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $m$ carrying a net positive charge $q$ is positioned on a smooth horizontal table that ends at a vertical wall, as shown in the figure. The block's distance from the wall is $d$. A horizontal electric field $E$ directed towards the right is turned on. Assuming any collisions to be elastic, determine the time period of the ensuing oscillatory motion and state if it is simple harmonic.
questions.solution:
Force on the block, $F = qE$

Acceleration of the block, $a = \dfrac{qE}{m}$

Let $t$ be the time taken by the block to reach the wall. Using the second equation of motion:

$d = \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$

$t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2d}{a}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2md}{qE}}$

Since the collision with the wall is elastic, the block rebounds with the same speed. The electric force continues to act towards the right, retarding the block's motion to the left. It will take the same time $t$ to come to rest at its initial position.

Total time period of oscillation, $T = 2t = 2\sqrt{\dfrac{2md}{qE}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{8md}{qE}}$

For a motion to be simple harmonic, the restoring force must be proportional to the displacement ($F \propto -x$). Here, the force is constant ($qE$) and always directed towards the right. Therefore, the motion is oscillatory but not simple harmonic.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform electric field of $10 \text{ N C}^{-1}$ exists in the vertically downward direction. Determine the increase in the electric potential when moving upward through a height of $50 \text{ cm}$.
questions.solution:
The relationship between electric field and potential difference is given by $\Delta V = -\vec{E} \cdot \Delta \vec{r}$.

Given that the electric field is in the vertically downward direction and the displacement is in the upward direction, the angle between $\vec{E}$ and $\Delta \vec{r}$ is $180^{\circ}$.

Magnitude of electric field, $E = 10 \text{ N C}^{-1}$.

Displacement, $\Delta r = 50 \text{ cm} = 0.5 \text{ m}$.

Increase in electric potential, $\Delta V = -E \Delta r \cos(180^{\circ}) = E \Delta r$.

Substituting the values, $\Delta V = 10 \times 0.5 = 5 \text{ V}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: To move a charge of $0.01 \text{ C}$ from point $A$ to point $B$ against an existing electric field, $12 \text{ J}$ of work must be performed. What is the potential difference $V_B - V_A$?
questions.solution:
The work done by an external agent in moving a charge $q$ from point $A$ to point $B$ against an electric field is given by $W = q(V_B - V_A)$.

Substituting the given values:

$12 = 0.01(V_B - V_A)$

$V_B - V_A = \dfrac{12}{0.01} = 1200 \text{ V}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two equal charges, each of $2.0 \times 10^{-7} \text{ C}$, are kept fixed at a separation of $20 \text{ cm}$. A third charge of equal magnitude is initially positioned midway between the two charges. It is subsequently moved to a point $20 \text{ cm}$ from both the charges. What is the amount of work done by the electric field during this process?
questions.solution:
Let the two fixed charges be $q_1$ and $q_2$, and the third charge be $q_3$.

Given $q_1 = q_2 = q_3 = q = 2.0 \times 10^{-7} \text{ C}$.

The initial position of $q_3$ is midway between $q_1$ and $q_2$. The distance from both charges is $r_{1i} = r_{2i} = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$.

The initial potential energy of the third charge is:

$U_i = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q_1 q_3}{r_{1i}} + \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q_2 q_3}{r_{2i}}$

$U_i = 9 \times 10^9 \times \left( \dfrac{(2.0 \times 10^{-7})^2}{0.1} + \dfrac{(2.0 \times 10^{-7})^2}{0.1} \right)$

$U_i = 9 \times 10^9 \times \left( \dfrac{4 \times 10^{-14}}{0.1} \times 2 \right) = 7.2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ J}$

The final position of $q_3$ is $20 \text{ cm}$ from both charges. The distance from both charges is $r_{1f} = r_{2f} = 20 \text{ cm} = 0.2 \text{ m}$.

The final potential energy of the third charge is:

$U_f = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q_1 q_3}{r_{1f}} + \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q_2 q_3}{r_{2f}}$

$U_f = 9 \times 10^9 \times \left( \dfrac{(2.0 \times 10^{-7})^2}{0.2} + \dfrac{(2.0 \times 10^{-7})^2}{0.2} \right)$

$U_f = 9 \times 10^9 \times \left( \dfrac{4 \times 10^{-14}}{0.2} \times 2 \right) = 3.6 \times 10^{-3} \text{ J}$

The work done by the electric field is equal to the negative of the change in potential energy:

$W = -\Delta U = U_i - U_f$

$W = 7.2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ J} - 3.6 \times 10^{-3} \text{ J} = 3.6 \times 10^{-3} \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
An electric field of $20 \text{ N C}^{-1}$ is present along the $x$-axis in space. Calculate the potential difference $V_B - V_A$ when the points $A$ and $B$ are given by:
(a) $A = (0, 0)$; $B = (4 \text{ m}, 2 \text{ m})$
(b) $A = (4 \text{ m}, 2 \text{ m})$; $B = (6 \text{ m}, 5 \text{ m})$
(c) $A = (0, 0)$; $B = (6 \text{ m}, 5 \text{ m})$
questions.solution:
The relation between potential difference and electric field is given by $V_B - V_A = -\int_{A}^{B} \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r}$.

Since the electric field is uniform and directed along the $x$-axis, $\vec{E} = 20 \hat{i} \text{ N C}^{-1}$.

The potential difference becomes $V_B - V_A = -E_x (x_B - x_A) = -20 (x_B - x_A)$.

For case (a):
$x_A = 0 \text{ m}$, $x_B = 4 \text{ m}$
$V_B - V_A = -20(4 - 0) = -80 \text{ V}$

For case (b):
$x_A = 4 \text{ m}$, $x_B = 6 \text{ m}$
$V_B - V_A = -20(6 - 4) = -40 \text{ V}$

For case (c):
$x_A = 0 \text{ m}$, $x_B = 6 \text{ m}$
$V_B - V_A = -20(6 - 0) = -120 \text{ V}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
An electric field of $20 \text{ N C}^{-1}$ is present along the $x$-axis in space. A charge of $-2.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ C}$ is transported from point $A$ to point $B$. Determine the change in electrical potential energy, $U_B - U_A$, for the cases (a), (b) and (c) where the coordinates of $A$ and $B$ are given by:
(a) $A = (0, 0)$; $B = (4 \text{ m}, 2 \text{ m})$
(b) $A = (4 \text{ m}, 2 \text{ m})$; $B = (6 \text{ m}, 5 \text{ m})$
(c) $A = (0, 0)$; $B = (6 \text{ m}, 5 \text{ m})$
questions.solution:
The change in electrical potential energy is given by the negative of the work done by the electric field.

$\Delta U = -W = -q \vec{E} \cdot \Delta \vec{r}$

Given $\vec{E} = 20 \hat{i} \text{ N C}^{-1}$ and $q = -2.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ C}$.

$\Delta U = -(-2.0 \times 10^{-4}) (20 \hat{i}) \cdot ((x_B - x_A)\hat{i} + (y_B - y_A)\hat{j})$

$\Delta U = 4.0 \times 10^{-3} (x_B - x_A) \text{ J}$

For case (a), $A = (0, 0)$ and $B = (4 \text{ m}, 2 \text{ m})$:
$\Delta U_a = 4.0 \times 10^{-3} (4 - 0) = 0.016 \text{ J}$

For case (b), $A = (4 \text{ m}, 2 \text{ m})$ and $B = (6 \text{ m}, 5 \text{ m})$:
$\Delta U_b = 4.0 \times 10^{-3} (6 - 4) = 0.008 \text{ J}$

For case (c), $A = (0, 0)$ and $B = (6 \text{ m}, 5 \text{ m})$:
$\Delta U_c = 4.0 \times 10^{-3} (6 - 0) = 0.024 \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electric field $\vec{E} = (\vec{i} \cdot 20 + \vec{j} \cdot 30) \text{ N C}^{-1}$ exists in a region of space. Assuming the potential at the origin is taken to be zero, determine the potential at the point $(2 \text{ m}, 2 \text{ m})$.
questions.solution:
The relationship between electric potential and a uniform electric field is given by:

$V - V_0 = -\vec{E} \cdot \vec{r}$

Given the electric field $\vec{E} = 20\hat{i} + 30\hat{j} \text{ N C}^{-1}$ and the position vector of the point $\vec{r} = 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} \text{ m}$.

Since the potential at the origin is $V_0 = 0$, the potential at the point $(2, 2)$ is:

$V = -(20\hat{i} + 30\hat{j}) \cdot (2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j})$

$V = -(20 \times 2 + 30 \times 2)$

$V = -(40 + 60) = -100 \text{ V}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electric field given by $\vec{E} = \vec{i} Ax$ is present in a region of space, where $A = 10 \text{ V m}^{-2}$. If the potential at $(10 \text{ m}, 20 \text{ m})$ is assumed to be zero, calculate the potential at the origin.
questions.solution:
The relation between electric field and potential is given by $dV = -\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r}$.

Given $\vec{E} = A x \hat{i}$, we have:

$dV = -(A x \hat{i}) \cdot (dx \hat{i} + dy \hat{j} + dz \hat{k}) = -A x dx$

Integrating both sides from the reference point $(10, 20)$ to the origin $(0, 0)$:

$\int_{V(10, 20)}^{V(0, 0)} dV = -\int_{10}^{0} A x dx$

$V(0, 0) - V(10, 20) = -A \left[ \dfrac{x^2}{2} \right]_{10}^{0}$

Substituting $V(10, 20) = 0$ and $A = 10 \text{ V m}^{-2}$:

$V(0, 0) - 0 = -10 \left( 0 - \dfrac{10^2}{2} \right)$

$V(0, 0) = -10 (-50) = 500 \text{ V}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The electric potential in a region of space is given by $V(x, y, z) = A(xy + yz + zx)$. Determine the dimensional formula of $A$.
questions.solution:
Electric potential is defined as work done per unit charge, $V = \dfrac{W}{q}$.

The dimensional formula of work $W$ is $[M L^2 T^{-2}]$ and that of charge $q$ is $[I T]$.

The dimensional formula of electric potential $V$ is $\dfrac{[M L^2 T^{-2}]}{[I T]} = [M L^2 T^{-3} I^{-1}]$.

Given the relation $V(x, y, z) = A(xy + yz + zx)$, the term $(xy + yz + zx)$ represents the product of two lengths, so its dimensional formula is $[L^2]$.

Using the principle of dimensional homogeneity, the dimensional formula of $A$ is:

$[A] = \dfrac{[V]}{[L^2]} = \dfrac{[M L^2 T^{-3} I^{-1}]}{[L^2]} = [M T^{-3} I^{-1}]$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The electric potential in a region of space is given by $V(x, y, z) = A(xy + yz + zx)$. Given that $A$ is $10$ SI units, determine the magnitude of the electric field at the point $(1 \text{ m}, 1 \text{ m}, 1 \text{ m})$.
questions.solution:
The electric field $\vec{E}$ is related to the electric potential $V$ by the negative gradient of the potential:

$\vec{E} = -\left( \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial x}\hat{i} + \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial y}\hat{j} + \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial z}\hat{k} \right)$

Given $V(x, y, z) = A(xy + yz + zx)$ and $A = 10$, we have:

$E_x = -\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial x} = -A(y + z)$

$E_y = -\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial y} = -A(x + z)$

$E_z = -\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial z} = -A(x + y)$

Substituting $x = 1$, $y = 1$, $z = 1$ and $A = 10$:

$E_x = -10(1 + 1) = -20$

$E_y = -10(1 + 1) = -20$

$E_z = -10(1 + 1) = -20$

The electric field vector is $\vec{E} = -20\hat{i} - 20\hat{j} - 20\hat{k}$.

The magnitude of the electric field is:

$|\vec{E}| = \sqrt{(-20)^2 + (-20)^2 + (-20)^2} = \sqrt{400 + 400 + 400} = \sqrt{1200} = 20\sqrt{3} \text{ N C}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two charged particles, each carrying a charge of $2.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ C}$, are moved from infinity to a separation of $10 \text{ cm}$. Determine the increase in the electric potential energy during this process.
questions.solution:
The initial electric potential energy of the system when the charges are at infinity is $U_i = 0$.

The final electric potential energy when the charges are separated by a distance $r$ is given by:

$U_f = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r}$

Given $q_1 = q_2 = 2.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ C}$ and $r = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$.

Substituting the values:

$U_f = (9 \times 10^9) \dfrac{(2.0 \times 10^{-5}) \times (2.0 \times 10^{-5})}{0.1}$

$U_f = 9 \times 10^9 \times \dfrac{4.0 \times 10^{-10}}{0.1}$

$U_f = \dfrac{3.6}{0.1} = 36 \text{ J}$

The increase in electric potential energy is $\Delta U = U_f - U_i = 36 \text{ J}$.

questions.q: The electric potential in a region of space is described by $V(x, y, z) = A(xy + yz + zx)$. Find the expression for the electric field.
questions.solution:
The electric field $\vec{E}$ is related to the electric potential $V$ by the negative gradient of the potential:

$\vec{E} = -\nabla V = -\left( \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial x}\hat{i} + \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial y}\hat{j} + \dfrac{\partial V}{\partial z}\hat{k} \right)$

Given $V(x, y, z) = A(xy + yz + zx)$

Calculating the partial derivatives:

$\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial x} = A(y + z)$

$\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial y} = A(x + z)$

$\dfrac{\partial V}{\partial z} = A(y + x)$

Substituting these into the expression for the electric field:

$\vec{E} = -A\{(y + z)\hat{i} + (z + x)\hat{j} + (x + y)\hat{k}\}$

$\vec{E} = -A\{\hat{i}(y + z) + \hat{j}(z + x) + \hat{k}(x + y)\}$

questions.q: Certain equipotential surfaces are depicted in the figure. Determine the magnitude and direction of the electric field in both situations.
options: (a) $200 \text{ V m}^{-1}$ making an angle of $60^\circ$ with the $x$-axis; (b) radially inward, decreasing as $E = \dfrac{6 \text{ V m}}{r^2}$
(a) $100 \text{ V m}^{-1}$ making an angle of $60^\circ$ with the $x$-axis; (b) radially inward, decreasing as $E = \dfrac{600 \text{ V m}}{r^2}$
(a) $200 \text{ V m}^{-1}$ making an angle of $120^\circ$ with the $x$-axis; (b) radially outward, decreasing as $E = \dfrac{6 \text{ V m}}{r^2}$
(a) $100 \text{ V m}^{-1}$ making an angle of $120^\circ$ with the $x$-axis; (b) radially outward, decreasing as $E = \dfrac{600 \text{ V m}}{r^2}$
questions.solution:
In situation (a), the equipotential lines are parallel, indicating a uniform electric field.

The perpendicular distance $\Delta r$ between the $10\text{ V}$ and $20\text{ V}$ lines is $\Delta r = (20\text{ cm} - 10\text{ cm}) \sin 30^\circ = 10 \times 0.5 = 5\text{ cm} = 0.05\text{ m}$.

Magnitude of electric field $E = \dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta r} = \dfrac{20 - 10}{0.05} = 200\text{ V m}^{-1}$.

The electric field is perpendicular to the equipotential lines and points towards decreasing potential (negative x-direction). Thus, the angle with the positive x-axis is $30^\circ + 90^\circ = 120^\circ$.

In situation (b), the equipotential surfaces are concentric circles. Observing the given values with $r$ in meters:

At $r = 0.1\text{ m}$, $V = 60\text{ V} \Rightarrow V \cdot r = 6$

At $r = 0.2\text{ m}$, $V = 30\text{ V} \Rightarrow V \cdot r = 6$

At $r = 0.3\text{ m}$, $V = 20\text{ V} \Rightarrow V \cdot r = 6$

Thus, the potential follows the relation $V = \dfrac{6}{r}$.

The magnitude of the electric field is $E = -\dfrac{dV}{dr} = -\dfrac{d}{dr}\left(\dfrac{6}{r}\right) = \dfrac{6}{r^2}$.

Since the potential decreases as the radial distance increases, the electric field points radially outward.

Answer: (a) $200 \text{ V m}^{-1}$ making an angle of $120^\circ$ with the $x$-axis; (b) radially outward, decreasing as $E = \dfrac{6 \text{ V m}}{r^2}$

questions.q: A circular ring of radius $r$ is uniformly charged with a linear charge density $\lambda$. Determine the electric potential at a point on the axis located at a distance $x$ from the centre of the ring. Subsequently, use this potential expression to determine the electric field at the same point.
questions.solution:
Consider an elemental charge $dq$ on the ring of radius $r$. The linear charge density is $\lambda$, so $dq = \lambda dl$.

The total charge on the ring is $Q = \int \lambda dl = \lambda (2\pi r)$.

The electric potential $V$ at a point on the axis at a distance $x$ from the centre is given by integrating the potential due to each elemental charge:

$V = \int \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{dq}{\sqrt{r^2 + x^2}}$

Since the distance $\sqrt{r^2 + x^2}$ is constant for all points on the ring:

$V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 \sqrt{r^2 + x^2}} \int dq = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 \sqrt{r^2 + x^2}}$

Substituting $Q = 2\pi r \lambda$:

$V = \dfrac{2\pi r \lambda}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 \sqrt{r^2 + x^2}} = \dfrac{r\lambda}{2\varepsilon_0 (r^2 + x^2)^{1/2}}$

The electric field $E$ along the axis is the negative gradient of the potential:

$E = -\dfrac{dV}{dx} = -\dfrac{d}{dx} \left( \dfrac{r\lambda}{2\varepsilon_0} (r^2 + x^2)^{-1/2} \right)$

$E = -\dfrac{r\lambda}{2\varepsilon_0} \left( -\dfrac{1}{2} (r^2 + x^2)^{-3/2} \times 2x \right)$

$E = \dfrac{r\lambda x}{2\varepsilon_0 (r^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$

questions.q:
As shown in the figure, an electric field of magnitude $1000 ext{ N C}^{-1}$ is established between two parallel plates separated by a distance of $2.0 ext{ cm}$. Evaluate the following:
(i) The potential difference between the two plates.
(ii) The minimum speed at which an electron must be projected from the lower plate in the direction of the field in order to reach the upper plate.
(iii) The maximum height attained by the electron if it is projected from the lower plate with the speed determined in (ii), but at an angle of $60^\circ$ relative to the electric field.
questions.solution:
Given:
Electric field, $E = 1000 \text{ N C}^{-1}$
Distance between plates, $d = 2.0 \text{ cm} = 0.02 \text{ m}$
Charge of an electron, $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$
Mass of an electron, $m = 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$

(i) The potential difference $V$ between the two plates is given by:
$V = E \times d$
$V = 1000 \times 0.02 = 20 \text{ V}$

(ii) The electron is projected from the lower plate in the direction of the electric field (upwards). The electric force on the electron is downwards, so it experiences a retardation $a = \dfrac{eE}{m}$.
For the electron to just reach the upper plate, its final velocity at distance $d$ must be zero. Using the third equation of motion:
$v^2 - u^2 = -2ad$
$0 - u^2 = -2 \left(\dfrac{eE}{m}\right) d$
$u = \sqrt{\dfrac{2eEd}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2eV}{m}}$
Substituting the values:
$u = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 20}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}}$
$u = \sqrt{\dfrac{64 \times 10^{-19}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}} \approx 2.65 \times 10^6 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

(iii) The electron is now projected at an angle of $\theta = 60^\circ$ relative to the electric field (which is vertical).
The vertical component of the initial velocity is:
$u_y = u \cos 60^\circ$
The maximum height $H$ attained by the electron depends only on its vertical component of velocity:
$H = \dfrac{u_y^2}{2a} = \dfrac{(u \cos 60^\circ)^2}{2a} = \left(\dfrac{u^2}{2a}\right) \cos^2 60^\circ$
From part (ii), we know that $\dfrac{u^2}{2a} = d = 2.0 \text{ cm}$.
$H = d \cos^2 60^\circ = 2.0 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2$
$H = 2.0 \times \dfrac{1}{4} = 0.50 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform field of $2.0 \text{ N C}^{-1}$ exists in space in the $x$-direction. Assuming the potential at the origin is zero, determine the expression for the potential at an arbitrary point $(x, y, z)$.
questions.solution:
The relation between electric potential and electric field is given by $dV = -\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r}$

Given $\vec{E} = 2.0 \hat{i} \text{ N C}^{-1}$ and $d\vec{r} = dx \hat{i} + dy \hat{j} + dz \hat{k}$

$dV = -(2.0 \hat{i}) \cdot (dx \hat{i} + dy \hat{j} + dz \hat{k}) = -2.0 dx$

Integrating from the origin $(0,0,0)$ to an arbitrary point $(x,y,z)$:

$\int_{0}^{V} dV = -\int_{0}^{x} 2.0 dx$

$V - 0 = -2.0 x$

Since $1 \text{ N C}^{-1} = 1 \text{ V m}^{-1}$, the expression for the potential at $(x,y,z)$ is $-(2.0 \text{ V m}^{-1}) x$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform field of $2.0 \text{ N C}^{-1}$ exists in space in the $x$-direction. Taking the potential at the origin to be zero, at which points is the potential equal to $25 \text{ V}$?
questions.solution:
The relation between electric potential and electric field is given by $dV = -\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r}$.

Given $\vec{E} = 2.0 \hat{i} \text{ N C}^{-1}$, the potential difference between a point $(x, y, z)$ and the origin $(0, 0, 0)$ is:

$V(x, y, z) - V(0, 0, 0) = -\int_{0}^{x} E_{x} dx$

$V(x, y, z) - 0 = -\int_{0}^{x} 2.0 dx$

$V(x, y, z) = -2.0 x$

We are given that the potential is $25 \text{ V}$. Substituting this value:

$25 = -2.0 x$

$x = -12.5 \text{ m}$

This equation represents a plane perpendicular to the $x$-axis. Thus, the potential is $25 \text{ V}$ at all points on the plane $x = -12.5 \text{ m}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform field of $2.0 \text{ N C}^{-1}$ exists in space in the $x$-direction. Determine the potential at the origin if the potential at infinity is taken to be zero, and state whether this choice is practical.
options: Negative infinity; it is not practical
questions.solution:
The electric field is given as $\vec{E} = 2.0 \hat{i} \text{ N C}^{-1}$.

The potential difference between the origin and infinity is given by the relation:

$V(0) - V(\infty) = -\int_{\infty}^{0} \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r}$

Given $V(\infty) = 0$, we have:

$V(0) - 0 = -\int_{\infty}^{0} 2.0 dx$

$V(0) = \int_{0}^{\infty} 2.0 dx = [2.0 x]_{0}^{\infty} = \infty$

Since the calculated potential at the origin is infinite, choosing the potential at infinity to be zero is not practical for a uniform electric field.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: As a charged particle travels from a point at a potential of $100 \text{ V}$ to a point at $200 \text{ V}$, its kinetic energy decreases by $10 \text{ J}$. Determine the charge on the particle.
questions.solution:
Using the principle of conservation of energy:

$\Delta K + \Delta U = 0$

Given that the kinetic energy decreases by $10 \text{ J}$, we have $\Delta K = -10 \text{ J}$.

Therefore, the change in potential energy is:

$\Delta U = -\Delta K = 10 \text{ J}$

The change in potential energy is also given by the relation:

$\Delta U = q(V_f - V_i)$

Substituting the given values $V_i = 100 \text{ V}$ and $V_f = 200 \text{ V}$:

$10 = q(200 - 100)$

$10 = 100q$

$q = 0.1 \text{ C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Calculate the work required to assemble three charged particles at the vertices of an equilateral triangle, as shown in the figure.
questions.solution:
The work required to assemble the system of charges is equal to the electrostatic potential energy of the system.

The potential energy $U$ of a system of three point charges is given by:
$U = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \left( \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r_{12}} + \dfrac{q_2 q_3}{r_{23}} + \dfrac{q_3 q_1}{r_{31}} \right)$

Given:
$q_1 = 2.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ C}$
$q_2 = 4.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ C}$
$q_3 = 3.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ C}$
$r_{12} = r_{23} = r_{31} = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$
$\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \text{ N m}^2/\text{C}^2$

Substituting the values:
$U = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9}{0.1} \left[ (2.0 \times 10^{-5})(4.0 \times 10^{-5}) + (4.0 \times 10^{-5})(3.0 \times 10^{-5}) + (3.0 \times 10^{-5})(2.0 \times 10^{-5}) \right]$

$U = 9 \times 10^{10} \left[ 8.0 \times 10^{-10} + 12.0 \times 10^{-10} + 6.0 \times 10^{-10} \right]$

$U = 9 \times 10^{10} \times (8.0 + 12.0 + 6.0) \times 10^{-10}$

$U = 9 \times 10^{10} \times 26 \times 10^{-10}$

$U = 9 \times 26$

$U = 234 \text{ J}$

Therefore, the work required to assemble the charges is $234 \text{ J}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform field of $2.0 \text{ N C}^{-1}$ exists in space in the $x$-direction. If the potential at the origin is set to $100 \text{ V}$, determine the expression for the potential at an arbitrary point $(x, y, z)$.
questions.solution:
The relation between electric potential and electric field is given by $dV = -\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r}$

Given $\vec{E} = 2.0 \hat{i} \text{ N C}^{-1}$ and $d\vec{r} = dx \hat{i} + dy \hat{j} + dz \hat{k}$

$dV = -(2.0 \hat{i}) \cdot (dx \hat{i} + dy \hat{j} + dz \hat{k}) = -2.0 dx$

Integrating both sides from the origin $(0,0,0)$ to an arbitrary point $(x,y,z)$:

$\int_{100}^{V} dV = \int_{0}^{x} -2.0 dx$

$V - 100 = -2.0 x$

$V = 100 - 2.0 x$

Since $1 \text{ N C}^{-1} = 1 \text{ V m}^{-1}$, the expression for the potential is $100 \text{ V} - (2.0 \text{ V m}^{-1}) x$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical particles, each with a mass of $10 \text{ g}$ and a charge of $2.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ C}$, are held at a separation of $10 \text{ cm}$ and subsequently released. Determine the speeds of the particles when the separation becomes large.
questions.solution:
Initial potential energy of the system is given by $U_i = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q^2}{r}$

Substituting the given values:

$U_i = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times (2.0 \times 10^{-4})^2}{0.1}$

$U_i = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-8}}{0.1} = 3600 \text{ J}$

When the separation becomes very large, the potential energy becomes zero and is entirely converted into the kinetic energy of the two particles.

By conservation of mechanical energy:

$U_i = K_f$

$3600 = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = mv^2$

$3600 = (10 \times 10^{-3}) v^2$

$v^2 = \dfrac{3600}{10^{-2}} = 360000$

$v = 600 \text{ m/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two particles, each with a mass of $50 \text{ g}$, possess opposite charges of $+4.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ C}$ and $-4.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ C}$. They are released from rest when the separation between them is $1.0 \text{ m}$. Determine the speeds of the particles once their separation is reduced to $50 \text{ cm}$.
questions.solution:
By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy:

$U_i + K_i = U_f + K_f$

Since the particles are released from rest and have equal masses, they will have equal speeds $v$ at any instant to conserve linear momentum.

$\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r_i} + 0 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r_f} + \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$

Substituting the given values $q_1 = 4.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ C}$, $q_2 = -4.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ C}$, $r_i = 1.0 \text{ m}$, $r_f = 0.5 \text{ m}$, and $m = 0.05 \text{ kg}$:

$mv^2 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} q_1 q_2 \left( \dfrac{1}{r_i} - \dfrac{1}{r_f} \right)$

$0.05 v^2 = (9 \times 10^9) (4.0 \times 10^{-5}) (-4.0 \times 10^{-5}) \left( \dfrac{1}{1.0} - \dfrac{1}{0.5} \right)$

$0.05 v^2 = (9 \times 10^9) (-16 \times 10^{-10}) (1 - 2)$

$0.05 v^2 = -14.4 \times (-1)$

$0.05 v^2 = 14.4$

$v^2 = \dfrac{14.4}{0.05} = 288$

$v = \sqrt{288} = 12\sqrt{2} \approx 16.97 \text{ m/s} \approx 17 \text{ m/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A sample of HCl gas is placed within an electric field of $2.5 \times 10^4 \text{ N C}^{-1}$. The dipole moment of each HCl molecule is $3.4 \times 10^{-30} \text{ C m}$. Determine the maximum torque that can act on a molecule.
questions.solution:
The torque acting on an electric dipole in a uniform electric field is given by $\tau = pE \sin \theta$, where $p$ is the dipole moment, $E$ is the electric field, and $\theta$ is the angle between the dipole moment and the electric field.

The torque is maximum when $\theta = 90^{\circ}$, which gives $\sin \theta = 1$.

$\tau_{\text{max}} = pE$

Given:
$p = 3.4 \times 10^{-30} \text{ C m}$
$E = 2.5 \times 10^4 \text{ N C}^{-1}$

Substituting the values:
$\tau_{\text{max}} = (3.4 \times 10^{-30}) \times (2.5 \times 10^4)$

$\tau_{\text{max}} = 8.5 \times 10^{-26} \text{ N m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two particles $A$ and $B$, possessing opposite charges of $+2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ and $-2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$, are positioned at a separation of $1.0 \text{ cm}$. Determine the electric dipole moment of this pair.
questions.solution:
The magnitude of each charge is $q = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$.

The separation distance between the charges is $d = 1.0 \text{ cm} = 1.0 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$.

The electric dipole moment $p$ is given by the product of the magnitude of either charge and the separation distance between them:

$p = q \times d$

$p = (2.0 \times 10^{-6}) \times (1.0 \times 10^{-2})$

$p = 2.0 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two particles $A$ and $B$, possessing opposite charges of $+2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ and $-2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$, are positioned at a separation of $1.0 \text{ cm}$. Determine the electric field at a point located on the axis of the dipole, $1.0 \text{ m}$ away from the centre.
questions.solution:
The dipole moment $p$ is given by $p = q \times 2a$

Substituting the given values:

$p = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 1.0 \times 10^{-2} = 2.0 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C m}$

The electric field on the axis of a short dipole ($r \gg a$) is given by:

$E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi \epsilon_0} \dfrac{2p}{r^3}$

Substituting the known values ($r = 1.0 \text{ m}$ and $\dfrac{1}{4\pi \epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \text{ N m}^2 \text{ C}^{-2}$):

$E = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 2 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-8}}{(1.0)^3}$

$E = 36 \times 10 = 360 \text{ N C}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three charges are placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle as illustrated in the figure. Determine the dipole moment of the combination.
options: $2 qd$, along the bisector of the angle at $2q$, away from the triangle
$\sqrt{3} qd$, along the bisector of the angle at $2q$, towards the triangle
$\sqrt{3} qd$, along the bisector of the angle at $2q$, away from the triangle
$qd$, along the bisector of the angle at $2q$, towards the triangle
questions.solution:
The system of charges can be considered as two electric dipoles by splitting the $2q$ charge into two $+q$ charges.

Let the vertices be $A$ (top, $-q$), $B$ (bottom-left, $2q$), and $C$ (bottom-right, $-q$).

The first dipole is formed by $-q$ at $A$ and $+q$ at $B$. Its dipole moment $\vec{p}_1$ has magnitude $qd$ and is directed from $A$ to $B$.

The second dipole is formed by $-q$ at $C$ and $+q$ at $B$. Its dipole moment $\vec{p}_2$ has magnitude $qd$ and is directed from $C$ to $B$.

The angle between the vectors $\vec{p}_1$ and $\vec{p}_2$ is $60^\circ$, which is the interior angle of the equilateral triangle at vertex $B$.

The resultant dipole moment $\vec{P}$ is the vector sum of $\vec{p}_1$ and $\vec{p}_2$.

The magnitude of the resultant dipole moment is given by:
$P = \sqrt{p_1^2 + p_2^2 + 2p_1 p_2 \cos(60^\circ)}$
$P = \sqrt{(qd)^2 + (qd)^2 + 2(qd)^2 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}$
$P = \sqrt{3(qd)^2} = \sqrt{3}qd$

Since the magnitudes of $\vec{p}_1$ and $\vec{p}_2$ are equal, the resultant vector $\vec{P}$ lies along the bisector of the angle between them.

Both $\vec{p}_1$ and $\vec{p}_2$ point towards vertex $B$. Therefore, their vector sum points from the inside of the triangle towards $B$ and continues outwards. This direction is along the bisector of the angle at $2q$, pointing away from the triangle.

Answer: $\sqrt{3} qd$, along the bisector of the angle at $2q$, away from the triangle

questions.q: Determine the magnitude of the electric field at point $P$ in the configurations illustrated in the figure for $d \gg a$. Assume $2qa = p$.
questions.solution:
For configuration (a):

The electric field at point P due to a point charge $q$ at distance $d$ is:

$E_a = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{q}{d^2}$

For configuration (b):

The system is an electric dipole with charges $-q$ and $+q$ separated by $2a$. Point P is on the equatorial line at distance $d$.

The electric field for $d \gg a$ is:

$E_b = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{p}{d^3}$

where $p = 2qa$ is the dipole moment.

For configuration (c):

The system has three charges: $-q$ at $x = -a$, $+q$ at $x = 0$, and $+q$ at $x = a$. Point P is at $(0, d)$.

The field due to the central charge $+q$ is:

$\vec{E}_1 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{q}{d^2} \hat{j}$

The field due to the charge $-q$ at $(-a, 0)$ is:

$\vec{E}_2 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{-q}{(a^2 + d^2)^{3/2}} (a\hat{i} + d\hat{j})$

The field due to the charge $+q$ at $(a, 0)$ is:

$\vec{E}_3 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{q}{(a^2 + d^2)^{3/2}} (-a\hat{i} + d\hat{j})$

The sum of the fields from the outer charges is:

$\vec{E}_2 + \vec{E}_3 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{q}{(a^2 + d^2)^{3/2}} (-2a\hat{i}) = -\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{p}{(a^2 + d^2)^{3/2}} \hat{i}$

For $d \gg a$, this approximates to:

$\vec{E}_{23} \approx -\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{p}{d^3} \hat{i}$

The total electric field at P is:

$\vec{E}_c = \vec{E}_1 + \vec{E}_{23} \approx -\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{p}{d^3} \hat{i} + \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{q}{d^2} \hat{j}$

The magnitude of the total electric field is:

$E_c = \sqrt{\left( \dfrac{p}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 d^3} \right)^2 + \left( \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 d^2} \right)^2} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 d^3} \sqrt{p^2 + q^2 d^2}$

Answer: (a) $\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 d^2}$
(b) $\dfrac{p}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 d^3}$
(c) $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 d^3}\sqrt{q^2 d^2 + p^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two particles with charges $-q$ and $+q$, each having mass $m$, are attached to the ends of a light rod of length $a$ to form a dipole. One end of the rod is clamped, and the system is positioned in a uniform electric field $E$ such that the dipole axis is aligned with the field. The rod is given a slight tilt and subsequently released. Ignoring gravity, determine the time period of small oscillations.
questions.solution:
Let the clamped end of the rod be the origin of rotation. Since one end is clamped, the mass $m$ at this end does not contribute to the moment of inertia.

The moment of inertia of the system about the clamped end is due entirely to the mass at the free end, which is at a distance $a$:
$I = ma^2$

When the dipole is in stable equilibrium, it is aligned with the uniform electric field $E$. If the rod is given a small angular displacement $\theta$, the charge at the free end experiences an electric force $F = qE$.

The restoring torque acting on the system about the clamped end is:
$\tau = -F a \sin\theta = -qE a \sin\theta$

For small oscillations, $\sin\theta \approx \theta$. Thus, the torque becomes:
$\tau \approx -qE a \theta$

Using the relation $\tau = I\alpha$, where $\alpha$ is the angular acceleration:
$ma^2 \alpha = -qE a \theta$

$\alpha = -\dfrac{qE}{ma} \theta$

This is the equation for simple harmonic motion, $\alpha = -\omega^2 \theta$, where the angular frequency $\omega$ is:
$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{qE}{ma}}$

The time period of small oscillations is given by $T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}$:
$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{ma}{qE}}$

questions.q: Estimate the number of free electrons in a copper wire possessing a mass of $64 \text{ g}$, assuming that each atom contributes one free electron (take the atomic weight of copper as $64 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$).
questions.solution:
Number of moles of copper is given by $n = \dfrac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Atomic weight}} = \dfrac{64}{64} = 1 \text{ mol}$

Number of copper atoms in $1 \text{ mol}$ is equal to Avogadro's number, $N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23}$

Since each copper atom contributes one free electron, the total number of free electrons is equal to the number of copper atoms.

Number of free electrons $= 6.02 \times 10^{23}$

questions.q: Two particles $A$ and $B$, possessing opposite charges of $+2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ and $-2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$, are positioned at a separation of $1.0 \text{ cm}$. Evaluate the electric field at a point located on the perpendicular bisector of the dipole, $1.0 \text{ m}$ away from the centre.
questions.solution:
Given charges $q = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ and separation $2a = 1.0 \text{ cm} = 10^{-2} \text{ m}$.

Dipole moment $p = q \times 2a = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 10^{-2} = 2.0 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C m}$.

Distance from the centre $r = 1.0 \text{ m}$.

Since $r \gg 2a$, the electric field at a point on the perpendicular bisector (equatorial plane) is given by $E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi \epsilon_0} \dfrac{p}{r^3}$.

Substituting the values:

$E = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-8}}{(1.0)^3}$

$E = 180 \text{ N C}^{-1}$.
